title: Electricity & magnetism
subtitle: Charges, fields and circuits
prerequisites: Foundations, Classical mechanics and Mathematical toolkit. Local links identify vectors, calculus, complex numbers and differential equations before they are used.

lessons.title: Charge has a sign, not a direction
lessons.idea: Charge can move between objects while the total charge of an isolated system stays the same.
body: Electric charge is a property that helps determine electrical interactions. There are two signs, positive and negative. These signs do not mean right and left. Same-sign charges repel; opposite-sign charges attract in the simple stationary point-charge model.

Ordinary atoms contain positive protons and negative electrons. A neutral atom has equal total positive and negative charge, not no charged parts. Removing an electron leaves the object more positive; adding one makes it more negative.

The coulomb, written C, is the charge unit. One electron has charge −e, where e is the positive elementary charge, exactly 1.602176634 × 10⁻¹⁹ C. For an isolated ordinary object gaining or losing whole electrons, its charge change is a whole-number multiple of e. Charge transferred out of one part appears elsewhere in the isolated system.
lessons.equation: Q_total = Q₁ + Q₂ + …;  ΔQ = n e
lessons.terms: Q_total, Q₁, Q₂: Total and individual charges (C). The subscripts label parts; signs show charge type. ΔQ: Change in the object’s charge (C). Final minus starting charge. n: Signed number of elementary-charge changes (no unit). Losing one electron gives n=+1; gaining one gives n=−1. e: Elementary-charge magnitude (C). Exactly 1.602176634×10⁻¹⁹ C by SI definition.

equationGuide.meaning: Add signed charges to find total charge. For transfer of whole electrons, the charge change is a signed whole-number count times the elementary charge.

example.title: Lose three electrons
steps: Start with a neutral object, Q = 0 C.
Losing three electrons gives ΔQ = +3e = +4.806529902 × 10⁻¹⁹ C.
The object becomes positive; the removed electrons carry the balancing negative charge elsewhere.

visual.title: Read the relationship
visual.caption: A charge-accounting summary, not a picture of electron paths.

check.prompt: A neutral object gains two electrons. What happens to its charge?
explanations: Electrons carry negative charge; gaining them does not add positive charge.
Correct. The object gains two negative elementary charges, so its charge becomes −2e.
Neutrality changes unless an equal positive charge is also added.

apply.title: Track the whole system
apply.text: Two initially neutral objects exchange electrons and end with one at +5e. What is the other’s charge if no charge leaves the pair?
apply.answer: It is −5e. Their signed total was zero and remains zero. This charge balance says nothing by itself about how much energy was transferred.

lessons.limits: The electron-transfer count describes ordinary isolated matter; a continuous charge density is a large-number approximation. Quarks have fractional elementary charges but are not isolated ordinary charge carriers in these examples.

glossary.definition: A signed property involved in electrical interactions.
A chosen set with no relevant exchange across its boundary; here no charge exchange.

lessons.title: Find the force between two small charges
lessons.idea: For stationary point charges, separation and charge size determine the electric force.
body: A point charge is a model that treats the charged object as having negligible size compared with the separation. Coulomb’s law gives the force size between two stationary point charges in vacuum.

Multiply the charge magnitudes, multiply by the electric constant kₑ, then divide by separation squared. Doubling separation makes the force one quarter as large. The bars around q₁q₂ mean use its nonnegative size for this magnitude formula.

Then choose direction separately: like signs repel and opposite signs attract, along the line joining the charges. Here kₑ ≈ 9.0 × 10⁹ N·m²/C² is a rounded constant. A microcoulomb, μC, is one millionth of a coulomb.
lessons.terms: F: Electric force (N). Bars mean magnitude only; decide attraction or repulsion from the charge signs. q₁, q₂: The two signed charges (C). Convert prefixes before substituting; 1 μC = 10⁻⁶ C. r: Separation between the model charges (m). Positive distance, not a signed coordinate. kₑ: Vacuum electric constant (N·m²/C²). Use the stated rounded value 9.0×10⁹ in the example.

equationGuide.meaning: Force magnitude is proportional to both charge sizes and falls as the square of the distance grows.

symbols.name: Electric force
symbols.description: Bars mean magnitude only; decide attraction or repulsion from the charge signs.

symbols.name: The two signed charges
symbols.description: Convert prefixes before substituting; 1 μC = 10⁻⁶ C.

symbols.name: Separation between the model charges
symbols.description: Positive distance, not a signed coordinate.

symbols.name: Vacuum electric constant
symbols.description: Use the stated rounded value 9.0×10⁹ in the example.

example.title: Opposite charges, separated
steps: Use q₁ = +2 μC, q₂ = −3 μC and r = 0.30 m.
The charges attract. Each experiences a 0.60 N force toward the other, not a negative force magnitude.

visual.title: Read the relationship
visual.caption: Point-charge force scaling in vacuum; direction comes from the signs.

check.prompt: With the same charges, separation increases from 0.30 m to 0.60 m. What is the new force size?
explanations: Inverse-square dependence gives a factor of four, not two.
Increasing separation weakens the force.
Correct. Doubling r multiplies r² by four, so0.60 N becomes 0.15 N.

apply.title: Check an approximation
apply.text: When would modelling two charged metal balls as point charges become questionable?
apply.answer: When their sizes are not small compared with separation, charge redistribution and geometry can matter. The centre-to-centre point formula is then not automatically an accurate contact-force prediction.

lessons.limits: Stationary point charges in vacuum; finite bodies, nearby materials and time-dependent effects can require other models. The formula is singular at r=0 and must not be used there.

glossary.definition: An ideal charge with negligible size for the calculation.
A quantity becomes one quarter when the relevant distance doubles.

lessons.title: Neutral matter can still respond to charge
lessons.idea: A neutral object can rearrange its charge without gaining any net charge.
body: In a conductor, some charge carriers can move through the material. In an insulator, charges are more tightly tied to their local surroundings. Neither label means the material contains only one sign of charge.

A nearby charged object can shift the positive and negative parts slightly relative to one another. This is polarization. The total can remain zero even though the charge distribution is no longer balanced in the same way at every place.
Keep two questions separate: did charge cross the object’s boundary, and did existing charge rearrange inside it? Rearrangement alone does not change the sum of all its positive and negative charges.
lessons.terms: Q_net: Net charge of the chosen object (C). The signed total, not the amount of each kind of charge. Q_positive, Q_negative: Positive and negative contributions (C). Q_negative already has a minus sign. Their spatial arrangement does not change their sum.

equationGuide.meaning: Add the signed positive and negative contributions. Equal-size opposite contributions give zero net charge even when they sit in different places.

symbols.name: Net charge of the chosen object
symbols.description: The signed total, not the amount of each kind of charge.

symbols.name: Positive and negative contributions
symbols.description: Q_negative already has a minus sign. Their spatial arrangement does not change their sum.

example.title: A neutral distribution changes
steps: A model object contains +6 nC and −6 nC; nC means10⁻⁹ C.
Its total is +6 nC + (−6 nC) =0 nC.
Moving the negative part slightly relative to the positive part changes the distribution, but the total remains0 nC if nothing leaves or enters.

visual.title: Read the relationship
visual.caption: Charge totals and charge arrangement are different descriptions; no microscopic path is asserted.

check.prompt: A neutral insulator polarizes without exchanging charge. What must happen to its net charge?
explanations: Correct. Polarization rearranges existing charge; it does not by itself add net charge.
A positive net charge would require a net change in charge balance.
A negative net charge would require a net change in charge balance.

apply.title: Explain an attraction carefully
apply.text: Does a neutral object’s attraction to a charged object prove that it gained net charge?
apply.answer: No. A nonuniform field can act differently on the separated parts of a polarized object, producing a net attraction while total charge stays zero. The result depends on the field and material response; neutrality alone does not mean no electrical interaction.

lessons.limits: Conductor/insulator are useful idealized categories, not universal statements at every temperature, field or timescale. This introduction does not calculate a material’s microscopic polarization.

glossary.definition: A shift in the arrangement of positive and negative charge.
A material with charge carriers able to move through it under the stated conditions.

lessons.title: Describe the field before choosing a probe
lessons.idea: Electric field tells us the force per unit positive test charge at a place.
body: A source charge affects the space around it. We describe that influence with an electric field E. At each position, E has a size and direction.

Define the direction using a small positive test charge: the field points the way that charge would be pushed. Small means its presence does not significantly rearrange the prescribed sources. Field is not the same quantity as force.

To find force on another charge q, multiply the field by that signed charge: F=qE. A negative q reverses the force direction. Doubling probe charge doubles force while the prescribed source field stays the same.
lessons.terms: E: Electric field vector (N/C). Newtons of force per coulomb of positive probe charge. F_test, q_test: Test force and positive test charge (N, C). The test charge is small enough not to alter the source arrangement significantly. F, q: Force and signed probe charge (N, C). The sign of q determines whether force follows or opposes E.

equationGuide.meaning: Divide test force by its positive test charge to describe the field; multiply that field by any chosen probe charge to predict its force.

symbols.name: Electric field vector
symbols.description: Newtons of force per coulomb of positive probe charge.

symbols.name: Test force and positive test charge
symbols.description: The test charge is small enough not to alter the source arrangement significantly.

symbols.name: Force and signed probe charge
symbols.description: The sign of q determines whether force follows or opposes E.

example.title: Same field, opposite charge
steps: To measure this field, a positive test charge q_test = 1 nC feels F_test = 2×10⁻⁷ N rightward. Divide: E = F_test/q_test = (2×10⁻⁷ N)/(1×10⁻⁹ C) = 200 N/C rightward.
Suppose E is 200 N/C rightward and a probe has q=−3 nC =−3×10⁻⁹ C.
F=qE gives (−3×10⁻⁹ C)(200 N/C)=−6×10⁻⁷ N along a right-positive axis.
The force is 0.60 micronewtons leftward. The field still points rightward.

visual.title: Read the relationship
visual.caption: Field and probe force are separate quantities. Field arrows are not particle trajectories.

check.prompt: In a fixed rightward field, a positive probe is replaced by an equal-size negative probe. What changes?
explanations: The prescribed sources did not change; their field does not reverse merely because the probe does.
Correct. F=qE changes sign when q changes sign.
A negative charge still experiences an electric force unless the field is zero.

apply.title: Compare descriptions
apply.text: Why is field useful when several different small probes visit the same place?
apply.answer: The source field is one shared description. Multiply it by each probe’s own signed charge to find that probe’s force, rather than defining a different source influence for every probe.

lessons.limits: Prescribed-source/test-charge approximation. A probe that strongly changes nearby conductors or other sources changes the physical problem. Field values depend on position and can also depend on time.

glossary.definition: A probe small enough not to substantially disturb the sources in this model.

lessons.title: A point charge gives a radial field
lessons.idea: The field of a stationary point charge points away from positive charge and toward negative charge.
body: Choose an observation point a distance r from a source charge Q. Coulomb’s law divided by a positive test charge gives electric-field size kₑ|Q|/r².

The vector rule includes direction with r-hat, a unit arrow pointing from source to observation point. A unit arrow has size 1 and no physical unit. Positive Q follows that outward arrow; negative Q reverses it.
The source field is specified without choosing the later probe charge. Only after finding E do we use F=qE for a particular probe. Never use a signed coordinate itself as the positive separation r.
lessons.terms: E: Electric field (N/C). A vector at the chosen observation point. Q: Source charge (C). Its sign controls outward or inward field direction. r, r̂: Separation and outward unit arrow (m, no unit). r is positive; r̂ points from source to observer. kₑ: Electric constant (N·m²/C²). Rounded to 9.0×10⁹ in this example.

equationGuide.meaning: Multiply the outward unit direction by the signed source charge and inverse-square factor to obtain the field vector.

symbols.name: Electric field
symbols.description: A vector at the chosen observation point.

symbols.name: Source charge
symbols.description: Its sign controls outward or inward field direction.

symbols.name: Separation and outward unit arrow
symbols.description: r is positive; r̂ points from source to observer.

symbols.name: Electric constant
symbols.description: Rounded to 9.0×10⁹ in this example.

example.title: A point to the right of a source
steps: Put Q=+2 nC at x=0 and observe at x=+0.30 m. Here r=0.30 m and r̂ points right.
Field magnitude is (9.0×10⁹)(2×10⁻⁹)/(0.30)² =200 N/C, with the numerical factors in the stated SI units.
The field points right. At x=−0.30 m it has the same size but points left.

visual.title: Read the relationship
visual.caption: Radial field directions are a mathematical diagram, not moving material or a probe path.

check.prompt: The same +2 nC source is observed 0.60 m to its left. What is the field?
explanations: Both distance scaling and direction are wrong.
The size is right, but positive-source field points away from the source.
Correct. The distance doubles, reducing 200 to 50 N/C, and the outward direction is left.

apply.title: Separate source and probe
apply.text: A negative probe is placed at that left-hand point. Which way is its force?
apply.answer: Rightward, opposite the leftward electric field. The field is 50 N/C leftward; multiplying by negative probe charge reverses the direction without changing the field itself.

lessons.limits: Stationary point source in vacuum with r>0. Near a finite source, use its actual charge distribution when the point approximation is inadequate.

glossary.definition: A direction arrow of size 1, used to carry direction without adding a physical unit.

lessons.title: Read an arrow, not a hidden path
lessons.idea: A field diagram tells us the field at places; it does not tell us the actual path of every charge.
body: An electric-field arrow gives direction for the force on a positive test charge at that place. Its drawn length may represent relative field strength if the diagram says so. A field line follows these local directions, but it is not a wire or thread.

A moving charge can have velocity in a different direction from the force. Its path follows the motion equations using both starting velocity and force. A negative charge is pushed opposite E, not automatically along a drawn line.

For one source in this point-charge model, field strength falls as1/r². An arrow twice as far away should therefore represent one quarter of the strength, not necessarily one quarter of a physical drawn length unless the scale is defined.
lessons.terms: E₁, E₂: Field magnitudes at two places (N/C). Use nonnegative sizes for this ratio. r₁, r₂: Positive distances from the same source (m). The source charge is unchanged and both distances use the same unit.

equationGuide.meaning: Compare field magnitudes at two distances: their ratio is the square of the inverse distance ratio.

symbols.name: Field magnitudes at two places
symbols.description: Use nonnegative sizes for this ratio.

symbols.name: Positive distances from the same source
symbols.description: The source charge is unchanged and both distances use the same unit.

example.title: Read relative strengths
steps: At r₁=0.20 m the field size is E₁=90 N/C. Compare with r₂=0.60 m.
The distance ratio is 0.20/0.60=1/3, so E₂/E₁=1/9.
E₂=10 N/C. This predicts strength; it does not specify a test particle’s starting velocity or path.

visual.title: Read the relationship
visual.caption: Conceptual arrow-reading rules; line density is meaningful only under a consistent drawing convention.

check.prompt: A positive moving charge has velocity across a field arrow. Must its velocity instantly align with the arrow?
options: No; the force changes velocity over time
Yes; a field line is its exact path
Only if its charge is negative
explanations: Correct. Acceleration follows force, but velocity changes continuously according to the motion model.
A field line is not generally a particle trajectory.
Changing charge sign reverses electric force, not this distinction between force and velocity.

apply.title: Audit a picture
apply.text: A drawing shows equally long field arrows at different distances from one isolated point charge. What should you check before concluding the field is uniform?
apply.answer: Check the diagram’s stated scale. Equal arrow lengths may show direction only. The physical point-charge field is not uniform; its strength changes with distance. A useful model must label what its visual marks encode.

lessons.limits: The ratio is for the magnitude of one unchanged point-source field in vacuum, away from its singularity. A multi-source field can cancel or vary in other ways.

glossary.definition: A drawn curve following local field direction, not a physical object or universal particle path.

practice.prompt: A positive point source gives 90 N/C rightward at a point0.20 m to its right. Keep the source fixed.

parts.label: Field magnitude0.40 m to its right
Field magnitude0.60 m to its right
Signed force on a −2 nC probe at 0.40 m
parts.feedback: Use right positive: (−2×10⁻⁹ C)(22.5 N/C)=−4.5×10⁻⁸ N.

practice.reasoning: Direction matters after the field calculation. Enter decimals or scientific notation, not fractions; tolerances permit numerical rounding and are not physical uncertainty estimates.

lessons.title: Add the fields with their directions
lessons.idea: Each prescribed source contributes a field; add those vectors before finding a probe’s force.
body: For prescribed charges, superposition means the total field is the vector sum of the fields from each source. Find each contribution at the same observation point. Do not add source distances or unsigned field sizes blindly.
Along one line, choose a positive direction and add signed values. In a plane, add matching x and y components separately. A zero total at one point does not mean every source field is absent there.
After adding E_total, a small probe of signed charge q feels force F=qE_total. The probe does not determine how the prescribed source fields are added.
lessons.equation: E_total = E₁ + E₂ + …;  F = q E_total
lessons.terms: E_total, E₁, E₂: Total and source fields (N/C). Each is a vector; in one dimension use signed components. q, F: Probe charge and force (C, N). F is the resulting vector force on the probe.

equationGuide.meaning: Add the source field vectors at the chosen place, then multiply the result by the probe’s signed charge.

symbols.name: Total and source fields
symbols.description: Each is a vector; in one dimension use signed components.

symbols.name: Probe charge and force
symbols.description: F is the resulting vector force on the probe.

example.title: A symmetric pair
steps: Place+2 nC at x=−0.30 m and +2 nC at x=+0.30 m; observe at x=0. Use kₑ≈9.0×10⁹ N·m²/C².
The left charge gives +200 N/C along a right-positive axis. The right charge gives −200 N/C.
Their sum is 0 N/C at the midpoint. Both individual fields are nonzero.

visual.title: Add two signed electric fields
visual.caption: Separate model case: fixed point sources at x = −0.5 m and +0.5 m in vacuum; kₑ ≈ 9×10⁹ N·m²/C². The observer cannot reach either singular source. nC means 10⁻⁹ C. The arrow shows direction only, not magnitude or a particle trajectory; positive x is right.

check.prompt: Only the right source doubles to +4 nC. What is the midpoint field now?
explanations: The larger right source pushes a positive probe leftward, not rightward.
Correct. Add+200 and −400 N/C to get −200 N/C.
The contributions no longer have equal size.

apply.title: Choose an axis first
apply.text: Why can adding200 N/C and 400 N/C as unsigned sizes give the wrong answer here?
apply.answer: Because the two contributions point opposite ways. Their directed sum has size 200 N/C, not600 N/C. Units alone cannot replace the direction information.

lessons.limits: Linear superposition for prescribed source fields in vacuum. Nearby responding materials can change the source distribution and require solving that response too.

glossary.definition: Adding the separate contributions under a model where they combine linearly.

lessons.title: A separated charge pair can turn in a field
lessons.idea: A neutral positive-negative pair can experience torque even when its net force is zero.
body: An ideal electric dipole consists of charges +q and −q separated by a small displacement d. The dipole-moment arrow p points from the negative charge toward the positive one and has size q times their separation.

In a uniform field, the two electric forces are equal and opposite, so their net force is zero. Unless the pair is aligned with the field, those forces act at different places and can turn the pair. Torque describes this turning effect.

The vector torque is p×E. Its size is pE sin θ, where θ is the angle between dipole and field. Potential energy U=−p·E, with zero chosen for a perpendicular pair, is lowest when p aligns with E. The dot and cross products are the mathematical toolkit operations, not new forces.
lessons.terms: q, d: Positive charge magnitude and separation vector (C, m). d points from negative to positive charge. p: Dipole moment vector (C·m). For its magnitude, p=qd uses positive q and separation length. E: Uniform electric field (N/C). The field is effectively the same at both charges. τ, U: Torque and potential energy (N·m, J). τ is tau. The scalar energy reference is zero when p and E are perpendicular. θ: Angle between dipole and field (radians or degrees consistently). Torque magnitude is pE sin θ; energy is −pE cos θ.

equationGuide.meaning: Charge size times separation gives dipole moment. Its across-field part determines torque, and its along-field part determines potential energy in this chosen reference.

symbols.name: Positive charge magnitude and separation vector
symbols.description: d points from negative to positive charge.

symbols.name: Dipole moment vector
symbols.description: For its magnitude, p=qd uses positive q and separation length.

symbols.name: Uniform electric field
symbols.description: The field is effectively the same at both charges.

symbols.name: Torque and potential energy
symbols.description: τ is tau. The scalar energy reference is zero when p and E are perpendicular.

symbols.name: Angle between dipole and field
symbols.description: Torque magnitude is pE sin θ; energy is −pE cos θ.

example.title: Turn a small pair
steps: Use q=2 nC, separation 0.040 m and a uniform field E=5,000 N/C. The dipole is perpendicular to the field.
Dipole magnitude is p=(2×10⁻⁹ C)(0.040 m)=8×10⁻¹¹ C·m. Torque size is pE=4×10⁻⁷ N·m because sin 90°=1.
The forces add to zero but their turning effects do not. At this orientation the stated potential-energy reference gives U=0 J.
If the same pair turns to align with the field, cos 0° = 1 and U = −pE = −4×10⁻⁷ J. This lower energy is relative to the stated perpendicular zero, not an absolute energy of all the sources.

visual.title: Read the relationship
visual.caption: A dipole is a charge-separation model. Its moment is not a particle velocity arrow.

check.prompt: The same pair is exactly opposite to the uniform field. What is its torque at that instant?
explanations: sin 180°=0, so the turning torque is zero at that exact orientation.
The uniform-field forces still cancel in their net force.
Correct. Torque is zero because sin 180°=0, but this high-energy alignment is unstable to a small turn.

apply.title: Distinguish force from torque
apply.text: Could a nonuniform field exert a net force on a neutral dipole?
apply.answer: Yes. The field can differ at the positive and negative charges, so their forces need not cancel. The simple uniform-field zero-force result cannot be used without checking that condition.

lessons.limits: Prescribed small charge pair and an approximately uniform external field for the displayed energy/torque model; changing separation or responding materials require more information.

glossary.definition: An equal-and-opposite charge pair separated in space.
The charge-separation vector pointing from negative toward positive.

lessons.title: Add contributions from a charged shape
lessons.idea: A continuous density lets us add the contributions from many small charge portions.
body: For a long object carrying many charges, it can be useful to spread the charge smoothly in a model. Line density λ means charge per length, in C/m. Surface density σ is in C/m² and volume density ρ is in C/m³. These are different kinds of density.
For a uniform thin line, a short length dx carries dq=λ dx. Add the electric field from each small dq using an integral. The observation distance usually differs from one source portion to another.

Put a positive line from x=0 to x=L and observe at x=−a, with a>0. Every contribution points left. Its distance is a+x. Integrating kₑλ/(a+x)² from 0 to L gives the displayed field magnitude. The symbol x inside the integral marks source position, not observation position.
lessons.terms: dq, λ, dx: Small source charge, line density and source length step (C, C/m, m). λ is lambda; continuous density averages over many discrete charges. a, L: Gap to the near end and line length (m). Both positive; the line runs from 0 to L and the observer is at−a. E, kₑ: Field and electric constant (N/C, N·m²/C²). The displayed magnitude is leftward for positive λ; use kₑ≈9.0×10⁹ in the example.

equationGuide.meaning: Multiply line charge density by a short length to get its charge. Add the inverse-square field contributions; the endpoint difference gives the field magnitude at the stated left-hand observation point.

symbols.name: Small source charge, line density and source length step
symbols.description: λ is lambda; continuous density averages over many discrete charges.

symbols.name: Gap to the near end and line length
symbols.description: Both positive; the line runs from 0 to L and the observer is at−a.

symbols.name: Field and electric constant
symbols.description: The displayed magnitude is leftward for positive λ; use kₑ≈9.0×10⁹ in the example.

example.title: A finite charged strip model
steps: Use λ=2 nC/m, L=0.30 m and a=0.30 m. Treat the strip as a thin line.
The endpoint difference is 1/(0.30 m)−1/(0.60 m)=1.6667 m⁻¹. Multiply by kₑλ=(9.0×10⁹)(2×10⁻⁹) N·m/C.
The field is about 30 N/C leftward. Using all the charge at the near-end distance would overestimate it.

visual.title: Read the relationship
visual.caption: Source contributions are added at one common observation point; no material is flowing along the integral.

check.prompt: Keep λ and L fixed but increase a from 0.30 m to 0.60 m. What is the new field magnitude?
explanations: Correct. The difference1/0.60−1/0.90 is about 0.5556 m⁻¹; multiplying by 18 N·m/C gives 10 N/C.
Moving farther away reduces every source contribution.
Increasing the gap cannot strengthen this positive-source axial field.

apply.title: Check the far limit
apply.text: When a is much larger than L, how should this line model compare with a point source?
apply.answer: The line’s total charge is Q=λL. Far away, all portions are at nearly the same distance, and the field approaches kₑQ/a² in magnitude. This limiting comparison checks the integral result; it is not exact at small gaps.

lessons.limits: Uniform thin-line charge with positive density for the displayed magnitude. The integral fails at a source singularity; a real finite cross-section and source redistribution can matter nearby.

glossary.definition: Charge divided by length, area or volume, as explicitly specified.
Replacing many separate small contributions with a smooth distribution.

lessons.title: Use symmetry before integrating
lessons.idea: On a uniformly charged ring’s axis, sideways field contributions cancel in pairs.
body: Imagine a thin ring of radius R carrying total charge Q uniformly around it. Observe at an axial coordinate z measured from the centre, perpendicular to the ring’s plane.

Each small portion contributes a field. A portion on one side has a partner opposite it. Their sideways components cancel, while their axial components add. All portions are the same distance √(R²+z²) from the observation point.

For a small ring charge dq in coulombs, its axial contribution is dE_z = kₑ z dq/(R²+z²)^(3/2), in N/C. The geometry factor is the same for every portion, so integrating around the ring gives ∫dE_z = [kₑ z/(R²+z²)^(3/2)]∫dq. The charge sum ∫dq is the total Q. This gives the displayed result.

The power 3/2 means the quantity times its square root. The sign of Qz sets the axial direction. At the centre z=0, every component cancels. This symmetry argument applies on the axis, not at an arbitrary off-axis point.
lessons.terms: E_z: Axial field component (N/C). Positive points along positive z; sideways components cancel on the axis. Q: Total ring charge (C). Uniformly spread around the ring. R, z: Ring radius and axial observation coordinate (m). R>0; z is signed and zero at the centre. kₑ: Electric constant (N·m²/C²). Rounded to 9.0×10⁹ in the example; the denominator has units m³.

equationGuide.meaning: The axial field equals the source-charge factor times axial distance, divided by the cube of the source-to-observer distance.

symbols.name: Axial field component
symbols.description: Positive points along positive z; sideways components cancel on the axis.

symbols.name: Total ring charge
symbols.description: Uniformly spread around the ring.

symbols.name: Ring radius and axial observation coordinate
symbols.description: R>0; z is signed and zero at the centre.

symbols.name: Electric constant
symbols.description: Rounded to 9.0×10⁹ in the example; the denominator has units m³.

example.title: An off-centre axial point
steps: Use Q=+3 nC, R=0.30 m and z=+0.40 m. The source-to-point distance is √(0.09+0.16)m=0.50 m.
The field points in positive z. This is not the same as placing all the charge at distance z from the point.

visual.title: Read the relationship
visual.caption: A symmetry summary for a thin ring’s axis, not a formula for an arbitrary off-axis point.

check.prompt: Move to z=−0.40 m without changing the positive ring. What is E_z?
explanations: The squared-distance denominator is unchanged but the numerator z changes sign.
Correct. Symmetry keeps the size and reverses the axial direction.
Only the central point has z=0 in this comparison.

apply.title: Check far away
apply.text: If |z| becomes much larger than R, what simpler source model should emerge?
apply.answer: The denominator approaches |z|³. The axial field approaches the signed point-charge field for total charge Q at the centre. This is a far-distance approximation, not a claim that the nearby ring behaves like a central point.

lessons.limits: Uniform thin ring in vacuum; formula only on its axis. It predicts a vector field, not an orbit or charge trajectory.

glossary.definition: A feature unchanged by a specified transformation, used here to match cancelling components.

practice.prompt: Use a uniformly charged ring with Q=+4 nC and R=0.30 m. Use rounded kₑ=9.0×10⁹ N·m²/C².

parts.label: Axial field component at z=+0.40 m
Axial field component at z=−0.40 m
parts.feedback: Changing z sign reverses the axial component, not its magnitude.

parts.label: Field magnitude at the centre
parts.feedback: Opposite source contributions cancel; z=0 makes the numerator zero.

practice.reasoning: The source-to-point distance is √(R²+z²), not just |z|. Tolerances permit decimal entry of the ideal example, not measurement uncertainty.

lessons.title: Count how strongly a field points through an area
lessons.idea: Electric flux combines field strength, area and the surface’s chosen orientation.
body: Draw a unit arrow perpendicular to a flat patch. It is the surface normal. Choose one of its two directions as positive. Flux is positive when the electric field points partly along that normal, negative when it points partly against it.
For a uniform field and a flat patch, multiply field magnitude E by area A and by cos θ. The angle θ is between field and normal, not between field and the flat surface itself.

For a curved surface or varying field, split it into small patches and add E·dA. Here dA is a small area arrow: its size is patch area and its direction is the chosen normal. Electric flux is not a flow of physical field-lines or charge.
lessons.equation: Φ_E = E A cos θ  (uniform field, flat area)
lessons.terms: Φ_E: Electric flux (N·m²/C). Phi-sub-E labels electric flux; the subscript distinguishes it from magnetic flux later. E, A: Field magnitude and patch area (N/C, m²). A here is area, not the ampere unit. θ: Angle between field and surface normal (degrees or radians consistently). cos θ includes the orientation sign.

equationGuide.meaning: Flux equals field strength times area times the share of the field pointing along the chosen normal.

symbols.name: Electric flux
symbols.description: Phi-sub-E labels electric flux; the subscript distinguishes it from magnetic flux later.

symbols.name: Field magnitude and patch area
symbols.description: A here is area, not the ampere unit.

symbols.name: Angle between field and surface normal
symbols.description: cos θ includes the orientation sign.

example.title: A tilted patch
steps: Use E=12 N/C, area A=0.50 m² and θ=60° from the chosen normal.
Flux is Φ_E=(12 N/C)(0.50 m²)cos 60°=3 N·m²/C.
Reverse the normal while keeping the same physical patch: the flux becomes −3 N·m²/C.

visual.title: Read the relationship
visual.caption: Flux is an oriented surface quantity. The normal arrow is a chosen mathematical direction.

check.prompt: The field and patch area stay fixed, but the field becomes parallel to the patch. What is flux?
explanations: A parallel-to-patch field has no normal component.
Negative flux requires a component opposite the chosen normal.
Correct. Field and normal are then perpendicular, so cos 90°=0.

apply.title: Read the right angle
apply.text: Why can using the angle to the surface itself give the wrong flux?
apply.answer: The formula uses the angle to the normal. If the stated angle is to the flat surface, its complement is the angle to the normal. State the geometry before choosing sine or cosine.

lessons.limits: The simple product needs a uniform field over a flat patch. General flux is a surface integral with consistent orientation.

glossary.definition: A direction perpendicular to the surface.
An oriented sum of how strongly a field points through a surface.

lessons.title: Enclosed charge sets closed-surface flux
lessons.idea: A closed surface’s total electric flux depends on the charge inside, not on the field at only one point.
body: A closed surface fully encloses a region, like a sphere or a box without holes. Its positive normal points outward. Add electric flux over the whole surface using that outward orientation.

Gauss’s law says this total equals enclosed charge Q_inside divided by vacuum permittivity ε₀. Permittivity is the constant that connects charge to electric-field response in vacuum; here ε₀≈8.85×10⁻¹² C²/(N·m²).

Outside charges can change the field at individual surface points. Their contributions to net flux cancel between inward and outward portions. Zero enclosed charge means zero total flux, not necessarily zero electric field everywhere.
lessons.terms: ∮ E·dA: Closed-surface electric flux (N·m²/C). The circle on the integral marks a closed surface here; the dot selects the normal component. Q_inside: Enclosed net charge (C). Add all signed charges inside; do not include charges outside. ε₀: Vacuum permittivity (C²/(N·m²), also F/m). Epsilon-zero is about 8.85×10⁻¹² in the stated SI units; it is not a charge.

equationGuide.meaning: Add the outward electric-flux contributions over the entire closed surface. The result is enclosed signed charge divided by vacuum permittivity.

symbols.name: Closed-surface electric flux
symbols.description: The circle on the integral marks a closed surface here; the dot selects the normal component.

symbols.name: Enclosed net charge
symbols.description: Add all signed charges inside; do not include charges outside.

symbols.name: Vacuum permittivity
symbols.description: Epsilon-zero is about 8.85×10⁻¹² in the stated SI units; it is not a charge.

example.title: A charge inside a closed box
steps: Suppose the box encloses Q_inside=+8.85×10⁻¹² C and use ε₀≈8.85×10⁻¹² C²/(N·m²).
The total flux is their ratio: +1 N·m²/C.
Changing the box shape without crossing any charge leaves this total unchanged, although the field distribution over the surface changes.

visual.title: Read the relationship
visual.caption: Gauss’s law fixes a whole-surface sum. It does not automatically provide the field at each point.

check.prompt: A closed surface encloses no charge but sits in a nonzero uniform field. Which statement is correct?
options: Net flux is zero, but field need not be zero
Field must vanish at every point
explanations: Correct. Equal inward and outward contributions cancel in the closed-surface total.
Gauss’s law constrains the sum, not every local field value separately.
With no enclosed charge, the signed total must be zero.

apply.title: Know what the law can solve
apply.text: Why is Gauss’s law alone not an easy formula for E at an arbitrary point near an irregular charged object?
apply.answer: It gives one total surface-flux constraint. Without enough symmetry, E varies over the surface and cannot simply be pulled outside the integral as one unknown constant. Other information or an explicit field calculation is needed.

lessons.limits: This vacuum relation uses total enclosed electric charge. Material descriptions using displacement field D and free charge require separate definitions; do not mix those formulas.

glossary.definition: A surface enclosing a region with no open boundary.
The constant relating charge to electric-field response in this vacuum model.

lessons.title: A sphere’s symmetry makes the flux useful
lessons.idea: Spherical symmetry makes the field magnitude constant on a concentric spherical surface.
body: For a spherically symmetric charge distribution, the field at a given radius points radially and has the same magnitude in every direction. A concentric Gaussian sphere therefore has total flux E×4πr².

Outside the charged sphere, all its charge Q is enclosed, giving E=kₑQ/r² as the signed outward component. Inside a uniformly charged solid sphere of radius R, enclosed charge is Q(r/R)³ because volume grows as radius cubed.

Inside that uniform solid sphere, the radial field is kₑQr/R³: it grows linearly from zero at the centre. A uniformly charged thin shell is different: it encloses no charge at interior radii, so its interior field is zero by symmetry and Gauss’s law.
lessons.equation: E_r = kₑQ/r² outside;  E_r = kₑQr/R³ inside a uniform solid sphere
lessons.terms: E_r: Signed outward radial field (N/C). Positive points outward; negative points inward. Q, R: Total charge and charged-sphere radius (C, m). R is fixed and positive; the inside rule assumes uniform volume density. r: Observation radius (m). The outside rule uses r≥R; the inside rule uses0≤r≤R. kₑ: Electric constant (N·m²/C²). Equivalent to 1/(4πε₀); about 9.0×10⁹ in this rounded example.

equationGuide.meaning: Outside, use all the source charge in the inverse-square law. Inside a uniformly charged solid sphere, use only the enclosed volume fraction, giving a field proportional to radius.

symbols.name: Signed outward radial field
symbols.description: Positive points outward; negative points inward.

symbols.name: Total charge and charged-sphere radius
symbols.description: R is fixed and positive; the inside rule assumes uniform volume density.

symbols.name: Observation radius
symbols.description: The outside rule uses r≥R; the inside rule uses0≤r≤R.

symbols.name: Electric constant

example.title: Inside a uniform solid sphere
steps: Use Q=+1 nC and R=0.20 m. Observe at r=0.10 m.
It points outward. For a thin shell with the same Q and R, the field at this interior radius would instead be0 N/C.

visual.title: Read the relationship
visual.caption: Uniform solid charge and a thin shell are different source models; the diagram summary is not a material cross-section.

check.prompt: In the same uniform solid sphere, move from r=0.10 m to r=0.05 m. What happens to field magnitude?
explanations: The interior solid-sphere rule is proportional to r, not inverse r.
Correct. The smaller Gaussian sphere encloses less charge; the field becomes 56.25 N/C.
The outside inverse-square formula cannot be used unchanged inside this source.

apply.title: Check the boundary
apply.text: Do the inside and outside solid-sphere formulas agree at r=R?
apply.answer: Yes. The inside expression becomes kₑQR/R³=kₑQ/R², matching the outside expression. This checks the field value for this uniformly filled sphere; a thin charged surface can instead have a jump in the normal field.

lessons.limits: Exact spherical symmetry in vacuum is required. A conductor in electrostatic equilibrium has a different charge distribution from a uniformly charged solid insulator. The centre’s field is zero even though a radial direction is undefined there.

glossary.definition: An imaginary closed surface chosen to apply Gauss’s law; not a new physical object.

practice.prompt: A uniform solid sphere has Q=+2 nC and R=0.20 m. Use rounded kₑ=9.0×10⁹ N·m²/C².

parts.label: Interior field if all charge instead forms a uniform thin shell
parts.feedback: For an ideal uniformly charged spherical shell, enclosed charge is zero inside and symmetry gives zero field.

practice.reasoning: State which source model you use before choosing the formula. The shell comparison changes the source distribution, not just the observation radius. Entry tolerances do not describe physical uncertainty.

lessons.title: Let symmetry choose the surface
lessons.idea: Different source symmetries lead to different distance dependence, even though Gauss’s law is the same.
body: An ideal infinitely long line has cylindrical symmetry. At distance r from the line, the field points radially and has one magnitude around a coaxial cylinder. Flux passes through the curved side; there is no flux through the end caps because the field runs along them. Let L be the cylinder length in metres. The curved-side area is 2πrL in square metres and enclosed charge is λL. For a positive line charge, Gauss’s law becomes E(2πrL)=λL/ε₀. The length L cancels when solving for E.

An ideal infinite uniform sheet has planar symmetry. Choose a short cylinder crossing the sheet, with equal faces on either side. The field points away from a positive sheet on both sides; the two faces contribute equally to outward flux. Let A be the area of each face in square metres. The two flux contributions total 2EA, while enclosed charge is σA. Thus 2EA=σA/ε₀; A cancels when solving for E.

The resulting magnitude rules differ: a line gives |λ|/(2πε₀r), while a sheet gives |σ|/(2ε₀). Line density λ is charge per metre; sheet density σ is charge per square metre. The ideal sheet field does not fall with distance, but a finite sheet only approximates this near its central region.
lessons.terms: E_line, E_sheet: Field magnitudes (N/C). Direction is away from positive source charge and toward negative source charge. λ, σ: Line and surface charge densities (C/m, C/m²). Lambda and sigma represent different kinds of density; their units are not interchangeable. r: Perpendicular distance from the line (m). Positive distance; no r occurs in the ideal infinite-sheet result. ε₀, π: Vacuum permittivity and pi (C²/(N·m²), no unit). Use ε₀≈8.85×10⁻¹² and π≈3.14159 for approximate numerical values.

equationGuide.meaning: For a long ideal line, divide charge per length by a circumference-related factor. For an infinite sheet, the two equal face contributions give a distance-independent magnitude.

symbols.description: Direction is away from positive source charge and toward negative source charge.

example.title: A long-line approximation
steps: Use λ=+2 nC/m and observe r=0.10 m from a line much longer than that distance.
The field points away from the line. The finite real line eventually departs from this ideal infinite-source formula.
For a separate positive infinite sheet with σ=4 nC/m², E_sheet=(4×10⁻⁹ C/m²)/(2×8.85×10⁻¹² C²/(N·m²))≈226 N/C.
This sheet field points outward on each side and has the same magnitude at different distances in the infinite-sheet model. It is not the same source geometry as the line.

visual.title: Read the relationship
visual.caption: Gauss-surface choice follows source symmetry. Infinite sources are idealizations, not claims about real-sized objects.

check.prompt: Move twice as far from an ideal infinite sheet, without crossing it or changing its charge density. What happens to field magnitude?
explanations: That distance rule belongs to an infinite line, not a sheet.
That inverse-square rule belongs to an isolated point-like source.
Correct. The infinite-sheet magnitude has no distance factor. A finite sheet need not behave this way far away.

apply.title: Check the units before calculating
apply.text: Why can the same numerical density not be substituted unchanged into both formulas?
apply.answer: Because λ counts charge per length and σ counts charge per area. Their dimensions differ. A value in C/m is not a value in C/m² merely because the written numbers match. The geometry and source definition must be specified.

lessons.limits: Infinite uniform line/sheet in vacuum. Finite-source approximations need observation distances small compared with the relevant extent and far from edge effects. Do not infer infinite total energy for a real finite object from an infinite idealization.

glossary.definition: The source looks unchanged under shifts along an ideal plane.
Sharing the same central axis.

lessons.title: Voltage compares energy per charge
lessons.idea: Voltage tells us how electric potential energy changes per unit of charge.
body: Voltage tells us how electric potential energy changes per unit of charge. It compares two places, not just one. A volt means one joule per coulomb.

Choose a start A and finish B. The change ΔV means V at B minus V at A. For a small fixed charge q, multiply q by this voltage change to get the change in its electric potential energy. Keep the sign of q: a negative charge reverses the energy-change sign.

In a stationary electric field, add the field component along each small displacement from A to B. Put a minus sign before this line integral to find ΔV. Electric-field work is the negative of the potential-energy change; work done by an external mover need not equal that change unless other energy changes are excluded.
lessons.equation: ΔU = qΔV; ΔV = −∫ from A to B E·dℓ; W_field = −ΔU
lessons.terms: ΔU, W_field: Potential-energy change and electric-field work (joules (J)). Δ means final minus initial. Positive electric-field work corresponds to a decrease of electric potential energy; it contributes positively to the probe’s kinetic-energy change, alongside work by any other forces. q: Probe charge (coulombs (C)). Signed and small enough not to change the source field appreciably. ΔV: Potential difference (volts (V = J/C)). Final potential minus starting potential. E, dℓ: Electric field and small directed path step (N/C, metres (m)). The dot product selects the along-path field; the integral adds these contributions. Bare-number arithmetic below uses the stated units; convert prefixes before combining unlike scales. Unit names: N is newton (force), J is joule (energy), m is metre (length), s is second (time); a squared metre is an area unit.

example.title: Work through a small model
steps: Take a uniform field of 8 N/C in the +x direction. Move 0.5 m in +x.
The voltage change is −(8 N/C)(0.5 m) = −4 V.

visual.title: Voltage compares energy per charge
visual.caption: Voltage change times charge gives energy change. Moving along the electric field lowers potential; the energy response also depends on charge sign.

check.prompt: Instead move q = −0.002 C through the same −4 V change. What is ΔU?
explanations: A negative charge times a negative voltage gives a positive result.
Divide neither quantity; multiply charge by voltage.

apply.title: Try a different situation
apply.text: Can a positive voltage change always be called an energy increase?
apply.answer: No. Electric potential energy increases for positive q but decreases for negative q. Voltage is a property of the source arrangement; energy also depends on the probe.

lessons.limits: Electrostatic sources and a nonperturbing probe are assumed. With changing magnetic fields, a path-independent voltage alone cannot describe all induced electric-field work.

equationGuide.meaning: Voltage change times charge gives energy change. Moving along the electric field lowers potential; the energy response also depends on charge sign.

lessons.title: Add potentials as signed numbers
lessons.idea: A point source gives an electric potential whose sign follows its charge.
body: A point source gives an electric potential whose sign follows its charge. Choose the potential to approach zero far away from a finite set of sources.

For one source, multiply its charge Q by the Coulomb constant k and divide by distance r. For several sources, add these signed numbers. Do not add arrows: potential is a scalar, while the electric field is a vector.

After finding V, multiply by a small probe charge q to get its interaction energy U with those fixed sources. A place can have zero potential but a nonzero field; a value and its spatial change are different things.
lessons.terms: V: Potential relative to infinity (V). A signed scalar, not a force. Σ, i: Sum and source label (no unit). Add one contribution for every source. k: Coulomb constant (N·m²/C²). Use 9.0×10⁹ for the rounded vacuum examples. Qᵢ, rᵢ: Source charge and distance to it (C, m). Distance is positive; source charge may have either sign. q, U: Probe charge and interaction energy (C, J). Sources are held fixed; this is not the total self-energy of all sources. Bare-number arithmetic below uses the stated units; convert prefixes before combining unlike scales. Unit names: N is newton (force), J is joule (energy), m is metre (length), s is second (time); a squared metre is an area unit.

example.title: Work through a small model
steps: A +2 nC source is 3 m from a point. A −1 nC source is 1 m from it. One nC is 10⁻⁹ C.
Using rounded k, their potentials are +6 V and −9 V.
Total potential is −3 V. A +0.002 C ideal probe would have interaction energy −0.006 J if it did not disturb the sources.

visual.title: Add potentials as signed numbers
visual.caption: Find each source’s signed contribution and add; multiply by the probe charge only when calculating its energy.

check.prompt: Keep the +2 nC source at 3 m, but place the −1 nC source 3 m away too. What is the total V?
explanations: The charge magnitudes do not cancel.
The negative source subtracts potential.
Correct: +6 V plus −3 V gives +3 V.

apply.title: Try a different situation
apply.text: Equal opposite charges are equally far from their midpoint. Does zero potential there imply zero field?
apply.answer: No. Their potentials cancel, but their field vectors at the midpoint point from the positive charge toward the negative one and add.

lessons.limits: Point sources, vacuum and finite nonzero distances are assumed. Infinity is not a usable zero reference for every infinite source distribution.

equationGuide.meaning: Find each source’s signed contribution and add; multiply by the probe charge only when calculating its energy.

lessons.title: The field follows the downhill potential slope
lessons.idea: A potential map lets us find the electric field by asking how rapidly potential changes with position.
body: A potential map lets us find the electric field by asking how rapidly potential changes with position. In one dimension, use the negative slope.

The derivative dV/dx measures volts changed per metre along x. Its negative is E_x, the signed x component of the field. In three dimensions, take each partial derivative; together they form the gradient ∇V. Negating that vector gives E.
The field points toward decreasing potential where the gradient is nonzero. This tells the force direction for a positive probe. A negative probe feels the opposite force.
lessons.terms: V, x: Potential and position (V, m). Potential is not the same quantity as electric field. E_x, E: Field component and full field (V/m = N/C). One volt per metre equals one newton per coulomb. d/dx, ∇: Derivative and gradient (per metre when applied here). The gradient collects the x, y and z slopes. Bare-number arithmetic below uses the stated units; convert prefixes before combining unlike scales. Unit names: N is newton (force), J is joule (energy), m is metre (length), s is second (time); a squared metre is an area unit.

example.title: Work through a small model
steps: Let V(x) = (2 V/m²)x².
Its slope is (4 V/m²)x, so E_x = −(4 V/m²)x.
At x = 3 m, E_x = −12 V/m: the field points toward decreasing x.

visual.title: The field follows the downhill potential slope
visual.caption: For each spatial direction, take the potential slope and reverse its sign.

check.prompt: For the same map at x = −2 m, what is E_x?
explanations: Correct: reversing the slope gives +8 V/m.
The slope is negative there, so its negative is positive.
A field needs volts per metre, not volts alone.

apply.title: Try a different situation
apply.text: What if 50 V is added to the whole potential map?
apply.answer: The field stays the same. The derivative of a constant is zero, so all potential differences and slopes remain unchanged.

lessons.limits: This scalar-potential-only relation applies to electrostatics in the stated region; a changing magnetic field requires an additional description of the electric field.

lessons.title: Moving sideways on a potential map
lessons.idea: An equipotential surface joins places with the same electric potential.
body: An equipotential surface joins places with the same electric potential. Moving along it gives zero voltage change, even when the field is not zero.

Where the field is nonzero and the surface is smooth, the field crosses the surface at a right angle. A field component along the surface would change potential along it, which would contradict its definition.

Zero electric work along the surface does not mean zero force. A perpendicular force can still change the direction of motion. Where the entire gradient is zero, the field is zero and there is no field direction to call perpendicular.

Zero here, not a claim about other forces. Bare-number arithmetic below uses the stated units; convert prefixes before combining unlike scales. Unit names: N is newton (force), J is joule (energy), m is metre (length), s is second (time); a squared metre is an area unit.

example.title: Work through a small model
steps: For V(x,y) = (5 V/m)x, lines x = constant are equipotentials in this plane.
Moving from (2 m, 1 m) to (2 m, 4 m) leaves V at 10 V.
The field is −5 V/m in x, perpendicular to the y-directed move, and its work is zero.

visual.caption: A move between equal-potential points changes no electric potential energy in this electrostatic model.

check.prompt: Move instead from x = 2 m to x = 3 m with q = +0.2 C. What is field work?
explanations: This move crosses equipotentials; ΔV is +5 V.
Correct: −qΔV = −(0.2)(5) = −1 joule.
That is the potential-energy increase, not field work.

apply.title: Try a different situation
apply.text: Can a region with constant potential everywhere have a nonzero electrostatic field?
apply.answer: No. All spatial slopes vanish, so E = −∇V is zero throughout that region.

practice.prompt: Use the electrostatic map V(x,y) = (3 V/m)x − (2 V/m)y. Move a +0.004 C probe from (0 m,0 m) to (2 m,1 m).

parts.feedback: Final V is 3×2 − 2×1 = 4 V; starting V is zero.

parts.feedback: Multiply +0.004 C by +4 V to get +0.016 J.

parts.feedback: Field work is the negative of the energy change: −0.016 J.

lessons.title: Charges settle until the metal’s field vanishes
lessons.idea: A conductor contains charges that can move through it.
body: A conductor contains charges that can move through it. Electrostatic equilibrium means the charge arrangement has stopped changing. If an electric field remained inside the conducting material, those charges would move, so the field inside must be zero.

With no internal field, there is no potential change through a connected piece of metal: it is an equipotential. Excess charge lies on its surfaces. At a smooth surface the field just outside is perpendicular, because a sideways field would move surface charge.

An empty closed cavity inside a conductor has zero electrostatic field when it contains no charge. If a charge is put in the cavity, the metal still has zero internal field, but the cavity generally does not. “Inside the metal” and “inside a hollow space” are different regions.
lessons.equation: In equilibrium metal: E = 0, ΔV = 0; just outside in vacuum: E_n = σ/ε₀
lessons.terms: E, E_n: Interior field and signed outward exterior component (N/C). The outward normal points out of the metal. ΔV: Potential difference through connected metal (V). Zero at equilibrium, not necessarily zero potential relative to infinity. σ: Local surface charge density (C/m²). Charge per surface area, signed. ε₀: Vacuum permittivity (F/m). About 8.854×10⁻¹²; F means farad, the capacitance unit introduced next. Bare-number arithmetic below uses the stated units; convert prefixes before combining unlike scales. Unit names: N is newton (force), J is joule (energy), m is metre (length), s is second (time); a squared metre is an area unit.

example.title: Work through a small model
steps: A connected conductor is held at +7 V relative to a chosen reference.
At equilibrium a point in its metal also has potential +7 V; the field in the metal is zero.
This is not a claim that the exterior field is zero or that the conductor has zero charge.

Exterior fields depend on the full charge arrangement.

apply.text: Why does the field just outside meet a smooth metal surface at a right angle?
apply.answer: A tangential component would drive mobile charges along the surface. In equilibrium that component vanishes; only the normal component can remain.

lessons.title: Geometry sets charge per volt
lessons.idea: A capacitor uses two separated conductors to hold equal and opposite charges.
body: A capacitor uses two separated conductors to hold equal and opposite charges. Capacitance says how much charge magnitude is stored for each volt between them. One farad is one coulomb per volt.

For fixed geometry in a linear medium, Q = CΔV uses positive charge magnitude Q and positive voltage magnitude ΔV. Capacitance depends on the shape, separation, surrounding material and electrical boundary conditions—not simply on the amount of charge added.

Two large parallel plates in vacuum have approximately C = ε₀A/d. More overlapping area A increases capacitance; a larger gap d reduces it. The gap must be small compared with plate widths so edge effects can be neglected.
lessons.terms: C: Capacitance (farads (F = C/V)). The symbol C here is a quantity; after a charge number C instead means coulombs. Q, ΔV: Charge and voltage magnitudes (coulombs (C), volts (V)). The two plates carry +Q and −Q. A, d: Overlapping plate area and gap (m², m). Both are positive. ε₀: Vacuum permittivity (F/m). About 8.854×10⁻¹² F/m. Bare-number arithmetic below uses the stated units; convert prefixes before combining unlike scales. Unit names: N is newton (force), J is joule (energy), m is metre (length), s is second (time); a squared metre is an area unit.

example.title: Work through a small model
steps: An ideal capacitor holds 18 microcoulombs at 6 V. A microcoulomb is 10⁻⁶ C.
C = 18/6 = 3 microfarads, where a microfarad is 10⁻⁶ F.
At the same geometry, doubling voltage doubles charge; it does not double C.
For a separate wide-plate model, A = 0.02 m² and d = 0.001 m give C ≈ (8.854×10⁻¹² F/m)(0.02 m²)/(0.001 m) = 1.7708×10⁻¹⁰ F, about 177 picofarads; pico means 10⁻¹².

check.prompt: For wide vacuum plates, double both area and gap. How does capacitance change?
explanations: Correct: the factor two in area cancels the factor two in gap.
The larger gap also matters.
The larger area also matters.

apply.title: Try a different situation
apply.text: An isolated capacitor keeps the same Q while its gap doubles. Neglect edges. What happens to its voltage?
apply.answer: Capacitance halves. Since ΔV = Q/C and Q stays fixed, voltage doubles. Moving the plates changes energy and may require mechanical work.

lessons.limits: Ideal separated conductors and fixed linear material response are assumed. Real devices have leakage, breakdown limits and edge fields. This is not a construction or electrical-safety guide.

lessons.title: Store energy and combine capacitors
lessons.idea: Charging a capacitor takes work because each additional small charge arrives against a larger voltage.
body: Charging a capacitor takes work because each additional small charge arrives against a larger voltage. For a linear capacitor with fixed C, the voltage rises from zero to Q/C. Adding the charging work gives stored energy Q²/(2C), also equal to C(ΔV)²/2. If z is the charge already moved, each small extra amount dz needs work (z/C)dz. Adding from z = 0 to Q gives ∫₀^Q (z/C)dz = Q²/(2C); z and dz are in coulombs and the integral is in joules.

Parallel means both capacitors connect across the same two nodes, or connection points. They share voltage and their charges add, so their capacitances add. Series means an unbranched chain with initially neutral isolated intermediate conductors. Each capacitor then has the same charge magnitude, and their voltages add.

Always state what stays fixed. At fixed voltage, a larger capacitance stores more energy. At fixed charge, a larger capacitance stores less energy. A connected source can exchange energy and charge, so do not treat a source-held voltage as an isolated capacitor.
lessons.terms: U: Stored electric energy (J). For fixed, positive, linear capacitance. Q, ΔV, C: Charge magnitude, voltage magnitude, capacitance (C, V, F). Use consistent base units when finding joules. C₁, C₂: Individual capacitances (F). Subscripts label the two devices. 1/C: Reciprocal capacitance (1/F). Divide one by the capacitance, not subtract it. Bare-number arithmetic below uses the stated units; convert prefixes before combining unlike scales. Unit names: N is newton (force), J is joule (energy), m is metre (length), s is second (time); a squared metre is an area unit.

example.title: Work through a small model
steps: Two ideal capacitors of 3 and 6 microfarads give 9 microfarads in parallel.
In series: 1/C = 1/3 + 1/6 per microfarad, so C = 2 microfarads.
At 4 V across that series pair, stored total energy is ½(2×10⁻⁶ F)(4 V)² = 16 microjoules; one microjoule is 10⁻⁶ J.

visual.caption: Stored energy is charging work; common voltage gives a sum for parallel, while common charge gives a reciprocal sum for series.

check.prompt: Keep the series pair isolated with its charge fixed, then halve its equivalent capacitance. What happens to stored energy?
explanations: That would apply to fixed voltage, not fixed charge.
Energy depends on capacitance even at fixed charge.
Correct: Q²/(2C) doubles when C halves at fixed Q.

apply.title: Try a different situation
apply.text: Why is series capacitance smaller than either positive individual capacitance?
apply.answer: For the same charge, the total voltage includes a drop across each device. More total voltage for the same charge means a smaller equivalent Q/ΔV.

lessons.limits: Series equal-charge reasoning assumes neutral intermediate nodes with no extra connections or trapped net charge. All capacitances are linear and positive; redistribution losses are not automatically zero.

lessons.title: A material changes the charging relationship
lessons.idea: A dielectric is an insulating material whose positive and negative charge distributions can shift slightly or turn.
body: A dielectric is an insulating material whose positive and negative charge distributions can shift slightly or turn. This polarization creates bound charge without requiring charge to flow freely through the material.

For a simple uniform linear dielectric filling a parallel-plate gap, capacitance becomes κ times its vacuum value C₀. The relative permittivity κ is a unit-free material factor. The material’s response reduces the field for a given free plate charge.

If the capacitor is disconnected so Q stays fixed, voltage falls by a factor κ. If an ideal source holds voltage fixed, extra free charge flows onto the plates instead. These are different experiments; the source must be included in the energy account for the second one.
lessons.equation: C = κC₀; fixed Q: ΔV = ΔV₀/κ; fixed ΔV: Q = κQ₀
lessons.terms: κ: Relative permittivity (no unit). Use κ ≥ 1, such as 4, for this ordinary static dielectric model; κ = 1 is the vacuum reference. C₀, C: Vacuum and filled capacitances (F). The gap is fully filled with the same geometry. Q₀, Q: Initial and final free plate-charge magnitudes (C). Bound material charge is distinct from free plate charge. ΔV₀, ΔV: Initial and final voltage magnitudes (V). Subscript zero means before insertion. Bare-number arithmetic below uses the stated units; convert prefixes before combining unlike scales. Unit names: N is newton (force), J is joule (energy), m is metre (length), s is second (time); a squared metre is an area unit.

example.title: Work through a small model
steps: An isolated 2 microfarad capacitor initially has 10 V, so Q = 20 microcoulombs.
Fill its gap with an ideal κ = 4 dielectric: C becomes 8 microfarads.
Q stays 20 microcoulombs, so voltage becomes 2.5 V. Stored energy falls from 100 to 25 microjoules; the energy difference can appear as mechanical work or other transfers during insertion.

explanations: Charge is not fixed when the source holds voltage.
Correct: 8 microfarads times 10 V gives 80 microcoulombs.
That incorrectly applies the voltage reduction to charge.

apply.title: Try a different situation
apply.text: Does polarization mean the dielectric must gain a net electric charge?
apply.answer: No. Positive and negative distributions can shift relative to one another while total material charge remains unchanged.

lessons.limits: Uniform fully filled linear material, electrostatic conditions and negligible edges are assumed. Frequency, temperature, losses, nonlinear response and dielectric breakdown can invalidate the constant-κ model.

lessons.title: Count signed charge passing each second
lessons.idea: Current measures how quickly signed charge crosses a chosen surface.
body: Current measures how quickly signed charge crosses a chosen surface. First choose which crossing direction counts as positive. An ampere means one coulomb per second.

For steady flow, divide transferred charge by elapsed time. For changing flow, I = dQ/dt gives the instantaneous rate; Q here is the accumulated signed charge that has crossed, not the charge sitting in a whole wire.

Conventional current points in the direction positive charge would move. Negative electrons drifting in the opposite direction can make the same conventional current. Charge is transferred, not used up as it passes a component.
lessons.equation: I_avg = ΔQ/Δt; I = dQ/dt; 1 A = 1 C/s
lessons.terms: I_avg, I: Average and instantaneous current (amperes (A)). Positive means the chosen conventional crossing direction. ΔQ, Q: Transferred charge and accumulated transferred charge (C). A negative charge crossing backward contributes positive signed transfer. Δt, t: Elapsed time and time (seconds (s)). Elapsed time is positive. Bare-number arithmetic below uses the stated units; convert prefixes before combining unlike scales. Unit names: N is newton (force), J is joule (energy), m is metre (length), s is second (time); a squared metre is an area unit.

steps: A total of +9 C crosses rightward in 3 s. Choose rightward as positive.
Average current is +9/3 = +3 A.

explanations: Correct: negative charge crossing forward gives −8/4 = −2 A.
The sign of the moving charge matters.
Divide transferred charge by elapsed time.

apply.title: Try a different situation
apply.text: Does 2 A entering a steady resistor become less current on leaving because energy was transferred?
apply.answer: No. In steady state with no charge accumulation, the same current leaves. Energy transfer does not mean charge disappears.

lessons.title: Connect microscopic motion to current
lessons.idea: Current density J tells us how much current crosses each square metre, including its direction.
body: Current density J tells us how much current crosses each square metre, including its direction. For one carrier type, multiply the number of carriers per volume n by charge per carrier q and their average drift velocity v_d.

Drift means the small average directed motion, not all the random motion of individual particles. For negative carriers, J points opposite the drift velocity. For a uniform wire cut perpendicular to J, the current is its along-normal component times cross-sectional area A.

A signal through a circuit is not carried by one electron making the whole journey first. Changes in electromagnetic fields spread through the arrangement; their speed depends on the materials and geometry and is not the usually much slower drift speed.
lessons.equation: J = nq v_d; I = J_n A for uniform normal flow
lessons.terms: J, J_n: Current-density vector and normal component (A/m²). Normal means perpendicular to the chosen cut. n: Carrier number density (1/m³). A positive count per volume. q: Charge of one carrier (C). Signed; negative for electrons. v_d: Mean drift velocity (m/s). A vector average, not the random speed. I, A: Current and cross-sectional area (A, m²). The letter A as a quantity here means area; as a unit it means ampere. Bare-number arithmetic below uses the stated units; convert prefixes before combining unlike scales. Unit names: N is newton (force), J is joule (energy), m is metre (length), s is second (time); a squared metre is an area unit.

example.title: Work through a small model
steps: Use a hypothetical carrier density n = 2×10²⁰ per m³, rounded electron charge q ≈ −1.6×10⁻¹⁹ C and drift −0.01 m/s along x.
Through a 0.5 m² cut with normal +x, I = +0.16 A. These are chosen model values, not a typical metal wire.

explanations: The same current density crosses more area.
Current density is unchanged, but total current is not.
Correct: I = J_n A doubles at fixed J_n.

apply.text: What if two kinds of mobile charge are present?
apply.answer: Find nq v_d for each kind and add the current-density vectors. Opposite charge signs do not automatically cancel because their drift directions also matter.

lessons.limits: The simple expression assumes a meaningful mean drift and known density. Uniform-area multiplication is replaced by a surface integral for nonuniform flow; this lesson does not model signal propagation quantitatively.

lessons.title: Track what enters, leaves, and builds up
lessons.idea: Charge conservation means charge inside a region can change only when charge crosses its boundary.
body: Charge conservation means charge inside a region can change only when charge crosses its boundary. If more conventional current enters than leaves, net charge builds up inside.

At a steady junction, charge is not accumulating. The total entering current must then equal the total leaving current. A junction is a connection where branches meet; it does not create or consume charge.

The local version uses charge density ρ and current density J. The time rate of density change plus the outward spreading of J is zero. The divergence ∇·J measures that local outward flow per volume; the equation states the same conservation rule in a very small region.
lessons.terms: Q_inside: Net charge inside the region (C). Not the total charge ever transferred through it. I_in, I_out, Σ: Entering current, leaving current, and sum (A). Add currents using the stated inward/outward signs. ρ: Volume charge density (C/m³). Signed charge per volume. ∂ρ/∂t: Local density-change rate (C/(m³·s)). Time derivative at a fixed place. ∇·J: Divergence of current density (A/m³). Positive means net current spreading outward locally. Bare-number arithmetic below uses the stated units; convert prefixes before combining unlike scales. Unit names: N is newton (force), J is joule (energy), m is metre (length), s is second (time); a squared metre is an area unit.

example.title: Work through a small model
steps: A region has 5 A entering and 3 A leaving.
Its net charge increases at 2 C/s. If those currents persist for 0.2 s, charge increases by 0.4 C.
At a steady junction this mismatch cannot persist: the branch currents must adjust or charge keeps accumulating.
Locally, if ∇·J = +2 A/m³, continuity requires ∂ρ/∂t = −2 C/(m³·s). Net outward current lowers the local signed charge density; an ampere is a coulomb per second.

Correct: 2 + 5 = 7 A, so no charge accumulates.
That would leave a 5 C/s accumulation rate.

apply.title: Try a different situation
apply.text: If incoming and outgoing currents are unequal for a short time, has charge conservation failed?
apply.answer: No. The difference is the rate of change of enclosed charge. The no-accumulation junction shortcut, not conservation itself, fails.

lessons.limits: Only charge crossing the specified boundary is counted. The steady-junction approximation is unsuitable when significant charge is accumulating in the chosen region.

lessons.title: A resistor links voltage drop to current
lessons.idea: A resistor transfers electrical energy as current passes through it.
body: A resistor transfers electrical energy as current passes through it. Choose positive current entering the higher-potential terminal. The positive voltage drop divided by current gives resistance at that operating point.

An ohmic model has constant resistance over the conditions being studied, so voltage drop is proportional to current. One ohm is one volt per ampere. Not every device follows a straight voltage–current relation.

For a uniform wire of length L and cross-sectional area A, resistance is ρL/A. Here ρ means resistivity, a material property—not the charge density used in the previous lesson. Resistivity can change with temperature; doubling voltage need not double current if heating changes the material significantly.
lessons.terms: ΔV, I: Voltage drop and current (V, A). Current enters the positive-drop terminal in this passive convention. R: Resistance (ohms (Ω = V/A)). Positive and constant only in the stated ohmic range. ρ: Resistivity (Ω·m). This lesson uses rho for a material property, not charge density. L, A: Wire length and cross-sectional area (m, m²). Uniform material and cross section are assumed. Bare-number arithmetic below uses the stated units; convert prefixes before combining unlike scales. Unit names: N is newton (force), J is joule (energy), m is metre (length), s is second (time); a squared metre is an area unit.

example.title: Work through a small model
steps: A model resistor has 12 V across it and carries 3 A.
If it stays ohmic at the same temperature, a 6 V drop gives I = 6/4 = 1.5 A.
Separately, a model material with ρ = 2×10⁻⁸ Ω·m, length 3 m and area 2×10⁻⁶ m² has R = ρL/A = 0.030 Ω. These are stipulated uniform-material values at fixed temperature.

visual.caption: For an ohmic element, voltage drop is current times resistance; a longer uniform wire resists more, and a wider one resists less.

check.prompt: A uniform wire’s length doubles and area halves while resistivity stays fixed. How does R change?
options: It becomes four times as large
explanations: Correct: doubling L and dividing A by two gives a factor four.
Both geometry changes increase resistance.
The reduced area adds another factor of two.

apply.title: Try a different situation
apply.text: Can one resistance measurement prove that a device is ohmic at all voltages?
apply.answer: No. It gives one operating-point ratio. Proportionality across a stated range, under controlled conditions such as temperature, must be checked separately.

lessons.limits: Uniform bulk-wire geometry and a suitable low-frequency ohmic regime are assumed. Real components have ratings, heating and non-ohmic limits; these examples are not instructions for live electrical work.
