lessons.title: Follow shared current and shared voltage
lessons.idea: Series resistors form a chain with no branching between them.
body: Series resistors form a chain with no branching between them. In steady state they carry the same current. Their voltage drops add, so their resistances add.

Parallel resistors connect to the same two nodes. They have the same voltage drop, while their currents add. Dividing each branch voltage by its resistance gives the reciprocal-sum rule for the equivalent resistance.

Equivalent resistance means one resistor would give the same terminal voltage–current relation. Check actual connections, not whether a drawing looks side-by-side. Some networks cannot be reduced using only these two rules.
lessons.terms: R₁, R₂: Individual resistances (Ω). Both are positive ideal ohmic values. R_series, R_parallel: Equivalent resistances (Ω). They describe different connections of the same devices. 1/R: Conductance, the reciprocal of resistance (1/Ω). Larger conductance means more current for the same voltage. Bare-number arithmetic below uses the stated units; convert prefixes before combining unlike scales. Unit names: N is newton (force), J is joule (energy), m is metre (length), s is second (time); a squared metre is an area unit.

example.title: Work through a small model
steps: Connect 6 Ω and 3 Ω in parallel. Their reciprocal sum is 1/6 + 1/3 = 1/2 per ohm, so the pair is 2 Ω.
Put a 4 Ω resistor in series with that pair: total resistance is 6 Ω.
With an ideal 18 V source, total current is 3 A. The parallel pair has 6 V across it, giving branch currents 1 A and 2 A.

check.prompt: Remove the 6 Ω parallel branch, leaving the 4 Ω and 3 Ω in series. What is total resistance?
explanations: The two remaining resistors are no longer parallel.
Correct: the only path passes through 4 Ω and 3 Ω, giving 7 Ω.
A reciprocal sum would describe a different connection.

apply.title: Try a different situation
apply.text: Why is a parallel pair’s equivalent resistance smaller than either positive branch resistance?
apply.answer: At the same voltage, both branches carry current, so the total is larger than either alone. The ratio voltage divided by total current is therefore smaller.

lessons.limits: Ideal wires, positive ohmic resistors and steady current are assumed. Internal source resistance and heating are omitted; equivalent resistance does not show where heat is produced.

lessons.title: Keep voltage signs consistent around a loop
lessons.idea: A loop is a path that returns to its starting node.
body: A loop is a path that returns to its starting node. In a lumped DC model, add every signed voltage rise and drop around it; the total is zero. Lumped means the wires and parts can be represented by a small set of nodes and components rather than a full changing field at every point.

Choose current directions and a loop-travel direction before writing signs. Crossing an ideal source from minus to plus gives +ℰ. Crossing a resistor in the assumed current direction gives −IR; crossing against it gives +IR. ℰ is called electromotive force, or emf, but it is energy supplied per charge, measured in volts—not a mechanical force.

Combine loop equations with steady junction balance. A negative solved current is useful information: the real conventional current is opposite the direction you guessed. It is not a negative amount of charge carriers.
lessons.terms: ΣΔV_loop: Sum of signed voltage changes (V). A complete trip ends at its starting potential in this model. ℰ: Ideal source emf (V = J/C). Source energy supplied per unit charge; not newtons. I, R: Assumed signed current and resistance (A, Ω). IR is the resistor voltage-drop magnitude when I is positive in the chosen direction. I_in, I_out: Junction currents (A). The steady rule assumes no net charge accumulation. Bare-number arithmetic below uses the stated units; convert prefixes before combining unlike scales. Unit names: N is newton (force), J is joule (energy), m is metre (length), s is second (time); a squared metre is an area unit.

example.title: Work through a small model
steps: In one loop, an 11 V source drives current through 2 Ω and 3 Ω resistors in series.
Travel through the source from minus to plus and then with the guessed current: 11 V − I(2 Ω) − I(3 Ω) = 0.

lessons.title: Decide who supplies energy
lessons.idea: Power is energy transferred each second.
body: Power is energy transferred each second. To track power at a component, label one terminal positive for voltage V and count current I as positive when it enters that terminal. Then absorbed power is P=VI. A positive result means energy enters the component; a negative result means it delivers energy to the rest of the circuit.

For a resistor with constant positive resistance R, voltage and current obey V=IR. Substituting gives P=I²R=V²/R, always nonnegative: electrical energy becomes thermal energy in this ideal account. These resistor formulas do not apply to every component. An ideal source delivering energy has negative absorbed power under the same terminal convention.

For constant power over elapsed time Δt, transferred energy is PΔt. Add absorbed powers of all components, including sources with their signs: a consistent ideal circuit account gives zero total. The sign convention records energy direction, not a negative amount of stored energy.

lessons.title: Watch the charging current fade
lessons.idea: An RC circuit joins a resistor R and capacitor C.
body: An RC circuit joins a resistor R and capacitor C. Start with the capacitor uncharged. At time zero connect them in series to an ideal source of constant positive voltage Vₛ. Let Q be the growing positive charge on the plate connected toward the source’s positive side; current I=dQ/dt flows into that plate.

The source voltage is split between resistor and capacitor: Vₛ=RI+Q/C. Therefore dQ/dt=(CVₛ−Q)/(RC). The difference CVₛ−Q shrinks at a rate proportional to itself, so it decays exponentially. Applying Q(0)=0 gives Q=CVₛ[1−e^(−t/RC)] and I=(Vₛ/R)e^(−t/RC). The number e is about 2.71828.

The time constant τ (tau) is RC, with seconds as its unit. After one τ the charge reaches about 63.2 percent of its final value and current falls to about 36.8 percent of its initial value. At the start Q=0; long afterward Q approaches CVₛ and current approaches zero. No charge jumps between capacitor plates in this ideal model.

body: Disconnect the source completely and connect a charged capacitor across one resistor. Let Q be the charge remaining on its initially positive plate, with Q(0)=Q₀>0. Define I_out as positive current leaving that plate. Charge conservation gives I_out=−dQ/dt.

The capacitor voltage Q/C drives the resistor current, so I_out=Q/(RC). Hence dQ/dt=−Q/(RC), giving Q=Q₀e^(−t/RC). Voltage and outward current decay by the same factor. This current is opposite to the earlier charging-current reference; a minus sign can reflect a reference direction rather than an impossible current.

At time zero the voltage is V₀=Q₀/C and I_out=V₀/R. Far later both approach zero. After each time interval RC the same fraction e⁻¹ remains—not the same fixed amount of charge. The capacitor’s lost stored energy becomes resistor heating in this ideal isolated circuit.

lessons.title: Account for energy during charging
lessons.idea: Charge an initially uncharged capacitor through a positive resistor from a constant ideal voltage source Vₛ.
body: Charge an initially uncharged capacitor through a positive resistor from a constant ideal voltage source Vₛ. The source supplies the same energy Vₛ per coulomb throughout charging. Total charge delivered is CVₛ, so total source work is CVₛ².

The capacitor voltage does not start at Vₛ: it rises from zero. To store a small additional charge dQ at charge Q requires work (Q/C)dQ. Adding this from Q=0 to Q=CVₛ gives stored energy ½CVₛ². The remaining half of the source work becomes heat in the resistor. Energy has not vanished.

Any finite positive R gives this final split in the ideal complete-charging model. Changing R changes the rate and duration, not the final energy split. Setting R exactly to zero invalidates this transient model: omitted inductance and other effects then matter. This result is not a claim about all possible ways to charge a capacitor.

lessons.idea: A charge q moving with velocity v in electric field E and magnetic field B feels force F=q(E+v×B).
body: A charge q moving with velocity v in electric field E and magnetic field B feels force F=q(E+v×B). The magnetic part uses a cross product, so it is perpendicular to both v and B when nonzero. Point right-hand fingers along v and curl toward B; the thumb gives v×B. Reverse that direction when q is negative.

The magnetic force size is |q|vB sin θ, where θ is the angle between velocity and field. Parallel motion gives zero magnetic force even when B is nonzero. A tesla measures magnetic field: one T is one N/(A·m). The axes used below have +x right, +y up, and +z out of the page.

Power transferred to a point charge is force dotted with velocity. Since v×B is perpendicular to v, the magnetic part alone does no work on that charge. It can change motion direction without changing speed. The electric part qE can change kinetic energy; zero magnetic work does not mean no magnetic force.

lessons.title: Use magnetic force to bend a path
lessons.idea: Let a particle enter a uniform magnetic field with velocity perpendicular to it and no electric field.
body: Let a particle enter a uniform magnetic field with velocity perpendicular to it and no electric field. The magnetic force stays sideways to motion. It supplies the inward acceleration needed for a circle without changing speed. Equate force sizes: |q|vB=mv²/r, then solve for radius r=mv/(|q|B).

The charge sign sets the bending direction, but the radius uses |q| and stays positive. If some velocity is parallel to B, that part continues unchanged while the perpendicular part circles, making a helix—a corkscrew-shaped path. The simple radius formula then uses only perpendicular speed.

Crossed electric and magnetic fields can instead cancel force for one direction and speed. When E is perpendicular to B and arranged opposite v×B, zero force requires E=vB, so selected speed is E/B. Cancelling sizes alone is insufficient: the vector directions must oppose.

lessons.title: Turn a current loop without a net push
lessons.idea: A straight wire segment carrying conventional current I in uniform B feels F=Iℓ×B.
body: A straight wire segment carrying conventional current I in uniform B feels F=Iℓ×B. The vector ℓ follows the current and has the segment length. This comes from adding qv×B over moving charges in the segment; conventional current already includes the carrier charge sign.

For a rectangular closed loop in a uniform field, opposite segments receive opposite forces, so total force is zero. Those forces can still turn the loop. To see the torque, orient the rectangle so its sides of length h are perpendicular to B and let it turn about that h direction. Opposite forces of size IBh act on those sides, separated by width w; their perpendicular separation for turning is w sin θ. Thus torque size is IBhw sin θ=IAB sin θ, where A=hw and θ is the angle between the loop’s normal and B.

Define magnetic dipole moment μ=NIA n̂ for N equal turns, where n̂ is a unit arrow normal to the loop. Curl right-hand fingers with the current; the thumb selects n̂. Torque is μ×B. It tends to align μ with B. μ here is a loop property, not the vacuum constant μ₀ or a micro-unit prefix.

lessons.title: Add magnetic contributions from a current path
lessons.idea: A steady current creates magnetic field around its path.
body: A steady current creates magnetic field around its path. To calculate the field at one observation point, split a thin wire into very short pieces. Each directed piece dℓ follows conventional current. Draw r from that source piece to the observation point; r̂ is a unit arrow in that direction and r is the distance.

The Biot–Savart rule gives dB=(μ₀I/4π)(dℓ×r̂)/r². The cross product determines direction; its size contains sin θ, where θ is the angle between current piece and observation direction. Add the vector contributions from the whole current path using an integral. Do not add their sizes unless their directions agree. Use μ₀ ≈ 4π×10⁻⁷ T·m/A as a rounded vacuum-permeability value for these calculations, not an exact modern SI definition.

For one short piece of an otherwise complete steady circuit, the finite approximation ΔB≈(μ₀/4π)IΔℓ sin θ/r² works when its length Δℓ is much smaller than its distance r. This is that piece’s contribution, not the total field of an isolated current that starts and stops in empty space.

lessons.title: Measure field around a long straight wire
lessons.idea: For a straight wire carrying steady current, the magnetic field circles the wire.
body: For a straight wire carrying steady current, the magnetic field circles the wire. Point the right thumb with the current; curled fingers show the field direction. For an ideal infinitely long thin wire, the field size depends only on perpendicular distance r from the wire, not position along it.

Here is how summing the small pieces changes the distance rule. Let u measure position along the wire from the point nearest the observer. The source-to-observer distance is √(r²+u²). Biot–Savart gives B=(μ₀I/4π)∫ from −∞ to +∞ of r du/(r²+u²)^(3/2). Its antiderivative is u/[r√(r²+u²)]; the endpoint difference is 2/r. Thus B=μ₀I/(2πr). Use μ₀ ≈ 4π×10⁻⁷ T·m/A as a rounded vacuum-permeability value for these calculations, not an exact modern SI definition.

For several wires, find each field’s direction at the observation point before adding. Two equal fields can cancel between parallel currents in the same direction, even though each wire creates a nonzero field. Real finite wires only approximate the infinite result far from their ends and outside their thickness.

lessons.title: Find a loop’s field along its centre line
lessons.idea: A circular current loop has an axis: the line through its centre perpendicular to its plane.
body: A circular current loop has an axis: the line through its centre perpendicular to its plane. At a point on that axis, sideways contributions from opposite wire pieces cancel. Their axial contributions add. The right-hand current rule chooses the positive axial direction.

Let a be loop radius and z signed distance along that axis. Every source piece is distance √(a²+z²) from the point. Projecting its Biot–Savart field onto the axis gives dB_z=(μ₀I/4π)a dℓ/(a²+z²)^(3/2). Summing dℓ around the loop gives circumference 2πa, so B_z=μ₀Ia²/[2(a²+z²)^(3/2)] for the chosen positive current direction. Use μ₀ ≈ 4π×10⁻⁷ T·m/A as a rounded vacuum-permeability value for these calculations, not an exact modern SI definition.

At the centre z=0 this becomes μ₀I/(2a). Far along the axis, where |z| is much larger than a, it approaches μ₀Ia²/(2|z|³). The 1/distance³ form is a far-field dipole approximation, not a replacement for the exact centre formula. The axial field points the same way on either side of this loop; its return path is elsewhere.

lessons.title: Count current through an oriented loop
lessons.idea: Magnetic circulation adds the field component along a closed imaginary path.
body: Magnetic circulation adds the field component along a closed imaginary path. Write it as ∮B·dℓ: the circle on the integral says go once around the whole closed path. This is not magnetic flux through an area. For steady currents in vacuum, Ampere’s law says this circulation equals μ₀ times the signed current passing through a surface bounded by that path.

Choose a normal arrow for the surface. Point your right thumb along it; curled fingers give positive path direction. Current through the surface along that normal counts positive and current against it counts negative. Add these currents to obtain I_enclosed. A current outside the surface can still affect the local B but cannot change this signed circulation total. Use μ₀ ≈ 4π×10⁻⁷ T·m/A as a rounded vacuum-permeability value for these calculations, not an exact modern SI definition.

The law does not automatically give B at one point. Only suitable symmetry lets you replace the integral by a constant B times path length. Zero enclosed current means zero circulation, not necessarily zero magnetic field. For time-changing electric fields, an additional term is required later; this lesson uses steady conditions.

lessons.idea: A solenoid is a coil with many turns spread along a straight length.
body: A solenoid is a coil with many turns spread along a straight length. For an ideal very long, closely wound coil, the interior field is nearly along the axis and nearly uniform away from the ends. The outside field becomes negligible in the infinite-length idealization; it is not exactly zero for a real finite coil.

Let n be turns per unit length. Choose an Ampere rectangle with one long side of length ℓ inside and the other outside. The short sides contribute negligibly because they run across the field. The inside side gives Bℓ and the enclosed current is (nℓ)I. Therefore B=μ₀nI. This calculation counts turns, not extra current created by the coil. Use μ₀ ≈ 4π×10⁻⁷ T·m/A as a rounded vacuum-permeability value for these calculations, not an exact modern SI definition.

Curl right-hand fingers along the winding current; the thumb points along the interior field. The field is not a material flowing down a pipe. Changing n or I changes the ideal field size; end effects and magnetic materials require additional modeling.

lessons.idea: A toroid is a coil wound around a ring-shaped region.
body: A toroid is a coil wound around a ring-shaped region. In the ideal continuously distributed winding, the magnetic field circles the ring’s central hole. At radius r inside the wound ring region, choose a circular Ampere path. Symmetry makes B tangent and constant on that circle.

The path length is 2πr and the signed enclosed current counts N winding turns, each carrying I. Thus B(2πr)=μ₀NI and B=μ₀NI/(2πr). Unlike a long straight solenoid’s interior estimate, this field varies across the ring thickness: smaller r gives larger B. Use μ₀ ≈ 4π×10⁻⁷ T·m/A as a rounded vacuum-permeability value for these calculations, not an exact modern SI definition.

In the ideal symmetric vacuum toroid, the central hole and region outside the winding have zero net enclosed current on their respective Ampere circles, and symmetry makes the field zero there. Real discrete windings and leads produce leakage fields. Zero enclosed current alone, without this symmetry, would not prove zero field.

lessons.terms: B(r): magnetic-field magnitude at radius r (T); Tangential in the ideal ring symmetry. r: distance from the toroid symmetry axis (m); Must lie within the wound ring region for this formula. N: number of winding turns (none); A count; not the force unit newton. I: winding current (A); Same steady current through every turn. μ₀: vacuum permeability (T·m/A); No magnetic core; use rounded value. π: pi (none); About 3.14159; 2πr is the Ampere circle length. A unit after a number is not a variable with the same letter. μ before a unit means one millionth; m before a unit such as mA means one thousandth. lessons.title: Turn changing magnetic flux into an emf
lessons.idea: Magnetic flux Φ_B measures the field component through an oriented surface, weighted by area: integrate B·dA.
body: Magnetic flux Φ_B measures the field component through an oriented surface, weighted by area: integrate B·dA. For a uniform field and flat area A, it is BA cos θ, where θ is the angle between B and the surface normal—not the surface itself. Flux uses webers: one Wb is one T·m².

Choose a loop direction and normal using the right hand: curled fingers follow the positive loop direction and thumb gives the normal. For a stationary loop, induced emf ℰ equals −dΦ_B/dt. Emf means energy supplied per unit charge around the loop; it is measured in volts, not newtons despite the historical word “force”. A volt is a weber per second. The minus sign links the loop direction to the sign of changing flux.

For N equal series turns all linking the same flux, ℰ=−N dΦ_B/dt. If flux increases in the positive normal direction, induced emf points in the negative loop direction. A current requires a conducting closed path; emf can be discussed without assuming a particular current. A moving loop also has a motional contribution, treated later.

A, dA: surface area and oriented area element (m²); The area arrow points along the chosen normal. θ: field-normal angle (rad or degrees); Cosine selects the through-surface component. ℰ: induced emf (V); Work per unit charge around the loop; not an ordinary conservative potential difference around a closed path. N: series turns linking equal flux (none); Count, not a newton. t, dΦ_B/dt: time and flux-change rate (s; Wb/s); One Wb/s equals one volt. ∫, ·: surface integral and dot product (operation); Add the normal field component over the surface. apply.text: If B remains constant but you merely reverse your chosen normal and loop direction, does the physical induction change?
apply.answer: No. The signed flux and signed emf labels both reverse; the physical situation is unchanged. For this stationary constant-area, constant-field loop, the flux rate and induced emf are zero under either convention.

lessons.title: Induction opposes a change in flux
lessons.idea: The induced response opposes the change of magnetic flux, not necessarily the existing magnetic field.
body: Choose a direction around the loop and the matching surface normal using the right-hand rule. Magnetic flux Φ_B is the signed field-through-area sum for that orientation. Faraday’s minus sign relates induced emf to how this signed flux changes.

In a closed resistive loop with no other voltage source and negligible self-inductance, increasing positive flux gives negative emf and therefore negative current. Negative means opposite the chosen positive loop direction. Its magnetic response tends to oppose the increase. Decreasing positive flux instead gives a response tending to support that flux. With appreciable inductance or a pre-existing current, the emf sign alone does not determine the instantaneous current direction.

Emf is energy supplied per charge around the loop, measured in volts; it is not a force in newtons. In a resistive loop the induced current can heat the resistor. The required energy comes from the agent or changing source responsible for the induction, not from creating energy out of nothing.
lessons.terms: ℰ: Induced electromotive force, or emf (volts (V)). The script E names energy transferred per charge around the loop, not the electric-field vector E. Φ_B, dΦ_B/dt: Magnetic flux and its time rate (webers (Wb), Wb/s = V). The chosen positive normal and loop direction must match. I, R: Signed current and positive resistance (amperes (A), ohms (Ω)). This simplified current rule neglects appreciable self-inductance and other circuit elements. Bare-number arithmetic below uses the stated units; convert prefixes before combining different scales. No, it tends to oppose the decrease
No emf can occur while flux decreases

Correct. The induced response tends to maintain positive flux while it is decreasing.
A nonzero rate of flux change can induce emf regardless of whether the signed flux rises or falls.

apply.text: An external agent moves a magnet near a resistive loop. The loop warms. What should an energy explanation include?
apply.answer: Include work done by the external agent and changes in field/source energy as well as resistor heating. The opposing magnetic response can require mechanical work. The simple flux rule alone does not mean the resistor’s heat appears without an energy source.

lessons.title: Motion can separate charges
lessons.idea: A moving conductor in a magnetic field can develop a voltage because charges feel magnetic force.
body: Consider a straight conducting bar of length ℓ moving at speed v across a uniform magnetic field B. Take the bar, motion and field directions to be mutually perpendicular. Charges moving with the bar feel qv×B, which shifts positive and negative charge toward opposite ends.

In an open bar after charge separation settles, the electric force balances the magnetic force along the bar. The resulting voltage magnitude is Bℓv. Its polarity follows v×B for positive charges, not a guessed sign.

If the bar forms part of a closed resistive circuit, current can flow and the bar feels a magnetic force opposing the driven motion in this ideal setup. Magnetic force does no work on an individual charge along its total velocity; the external mechanical drive supplies the circuit’s energy.

Ell is length along the bar; motion is perpendicular to both bar and field. ℰ, I, R: Emf, current magnitude and circuit resistance (V, A, Ω). Signs/polarity need the cross-product direction; these displayed expressions give magnitudes. Bare-number arithmetic below uses the stated units; convert prefixes before combining different scales. lessons.title: One changing current can induce emf in another circuit
lessons.idea: Magnetic coupling transfers effects between circuits without requiring charge to cross between their wires.
body: A changing current in one coil can change magnetic flux through another. Mutual inductance M measures the flux linkage of one circuit per current in the other for a fixed linear geometry. Flux linkage means adding the flux through every turn.

With a specified orientation, induced emf in coil 2 is −M dI₁/dt. The minus sign and chosen winding directions must be read together; reversing the labelled terminals changes the reported voltage sign.

An ideal transformer assumes both windings share the same changing core flux, with negligible losses and leakage. The voltage magnitude ratio is the turns ratio. Conservation of power then gives the inverse current ratio. A steady unchanging flux does not produce transformer emf.
lessons.terms: M: Mutual inductance (henries (H)). One henry times one ampere per second gives one volt. Geometry and winding signs are specified. I₁, ℰ₂: Primary current and secondary induced emf (A, V). Subscripts label circuits; dI₁/dt is in A/s. N₁, N₂: Numbers of winding turns (no unit). N here is a count, not the newton unit. V₁, V₂, I₂: Winding voltages and secondary current (V, A). Use consistent amplitudes or RMS values; ratios here are magnitudes in the ideal model. Bare-number arithmetic below uses the stated units; convert prefixes before combining different scales. The secondary RMS voltage is 12 V ×30/120=3 V. If the resistive load draws 0.60 A RMS, output power is 1.8 W.

lessons.title: A circuit can oppose changes in its own current
lessons.idea: An inductor stores magnetic-field energy and develops an emf when its current changes.
body: A current creates magnetic flux. For a fixed linear coil, total flux linkage is proportional to its current: NΦ_B=LI. Self-inductance L is that proportionality, measured in henries. It belongs to the geometry and material response under the stated approximation.
A changing current changes the coil’s own flux linkage. Its induced emf is −L dI/dt when L is constant. This back emf opposes the current change, not necessarily the current itself.

To build the current, an external source transfers energy into the magnetic field. Adding the required power over the charging process gives U_L=½LI². When current falls, that stored energy can be returned or transferred elsewhere. An ideal inductor does not continuously dissipate power like a resistor.
lessons.terms: ℰ_self: Self-induced emf (V). The sign follows the chosen current/loop orientation. L: Constant self-inductance (H). H = V·s/A; not the length symbol used in earlier geometry. I, dI/dt: Current and its rate of change (A, A/s). The energy depends on I², so it is nonnegative for positive L. U_L: Stored magnetic energy (J). ½ means one half. H·A² equals joules. apply.title: Explain the work integral
apply.text: How does adding work while current grows lead to½LI²?
apply.answer: The source must supply power P=LI(dI/dt) to an otherwise ideal inductor. Here P is in watts, L in henries and I in amperes. Integrate over time: the energy increase is ∫₀ᴵ L I′ dI′=½LI², where I′ is a temporary current variable. This assumes constant L and zero starting current.

lessons.title: An inductor prevents an ideal current jump
lessons.idea: An ideal resistor-inductor circuit changes current over a time scale set by L/R.
body: For an ideal DC source V_s connected to a series resistor R and inductor L, the loop balance is L dI/dt + RI = V_s. The resistor’s voltage depends on current; the inductor’s voltage depends on how quickly current changes.
Starting from zero current, the solution is I=(V_s/R)(1−e^(−t/τ)), with τ=L/R. The constant e is about 2.718. At one time constant, current is about 63.2 percent of its eventual value V_s/R.

If the source is removed but a closed R-L path remains, the current instead decays from I₀ as I=I₀e^(−t/τ). This is not an ideal open circuit: stored inductor energy needs an accounted-for path or field response.
lessons.terms: τ, t: Time constant and elapsed time (s). Tau=L/R. The ratio t/τ has no unit. L, R: Inductance and resistance (H, Ω). Positive constants in this linear model. V_s, I₀: Source voltage and starting decay current (V, A). Rise formula starts at zero current; decay starts at I₀. I_rise, I_decay: Current for the two distinct setups (A). example.title: Watch the first time constant
steps: Use L=0.60 H, R=3.0 Ω and V_s=6.0 V, with initial current zero.
τ=(0.60 H)/(3.0 Ω)=0.20 s and final current is 6.0 V/3.0 Ω=2.0 A.
At t=0.20 s, I=2(1−1/e) A≈1.264 A. The current has not instantly jumped to 2 A.

For a separate decay case, start from I₀=2.0 A and remove the source while keeping the same closed R-L path. After 0.20 s, current is (2.0 A)e⁻¹≈0.736 A in its original direction; it is decreasing, not instantly zero.

check.prompt: Keep L fixed and double R. What happens to τ=L/R?
explanations: Correct. Dividing by twice the resistance gives half the time constant. The driven final current also changes if V_s is fixed.
That would follow if L doubled with R fixed, not this change.
The time constant explicitly depends on R.

apply.title: Check ideal switching limits
apply.text: Why does the decay formula not describe simply removing every possible current path instantaneously?
apply.answer: It assumes a closed path containing R and L. An ideal instantaneous interruption of nonzero inductor current would demand an unbounded rate of change and is outside that simple solution. Real systems respond through other paths, capacitance, fields or breakdown; this lesson does not prescribe a switching design.

lessons.limits: Lumped linear circuit, constant source/R/L, negligible parasitic effects and the specified switch topology. No practical high-voltage switching or safety instruction.

The characteristic exponential-response time, not the exact time at which a process finishes.

lessons.title: Energy can move between electric and magnetic storage
lessons.idea: An ideal capacitor and inductor exchange energy while total stored energy stays constant.
body: A capacitor stores electric energy and an inductor stores magnetic energy. With no resistance or outside drive, an ideal L-C loop can exchange energy between the two.

Let q be signed charge on a chosen capacitor plate, and choose current I=dq/dt into that plate. The loop equation is L d²q/dt² + q/C = 0. It has the oscillator form taught in the mathematical toolkit, with angular frequency ω₀=1/√(LC).

If charge starts at Q with zero current, q=Q cos(ω₀t) and I=−ω₀Q sin(ω₀t). Charge energy q²/(2C) and magnetic energy LI²/2 add to the constant Q²/(2C). Negative current simply means charge on the chosen plate is decreasing.
lessons.terms: L, C: Inductance and capacitance (H, F). Positive constants. C here names capacitance, not the coulomb unit symbol after a number. ω₀, t: Natural angular frequency and time (rad/s, s). ω₀t is an angle in radians, dimensionless in the trigonometric function. Q, q(t): Starting maximum charge and current plate charge (coulombs (C)). Q is an amplitude; q may be positive or negative. I(t): Signed current into the chosen plate (A). It equals dq/dt with this explicitly chosen sign. Bare-number arithmetic below uses the stated units; convert prefixes before combining different scales. options: Yes, because the capacitor is empty
No, magnetic energy can be maximum
Only if the charge was initially positive
explanations: That ignores energy in the inductor.
Correct. In this ideal oscillation, energy can be entirely magnetic when q=0.
The sign of the initial charge does not remove magnetic storage.

apply.title: Separate frequency from period
apply.text: For ω₀=10 rad/s, what is the oscillation period?
apply.answer: Period T is the time for a full 2π-radian cycle, so T=2π/ω₀≈0.628 s. Frequency f=1/T≈1.59 Hz means cycles per second. Angular frequency in rad/s and frequency in Hz are different numerical conventions for the same repeating motion.

lessons.title: A driven circuit can lag or lead its source
lessons.idea: In a series RLC circuit, resistance and opposing reactances together set the sinusoidal current.
body: Use a series resistor R, inductor L and capacitor C driven at a fixed angular frequency ω. After transients decay, the steady current is sinusoidal. Complex phasors, taught in the toolkit, track its size and phase without treating complex numbers as directly measured current.

With the e^(iωt) convention, impedance is Z=R+i(ωL−1/(ωC)), in ohms. The imaginary parts represent the different timing of inductor and capacitor responses. Magnitude |Z|=√[R²+(ωL−1/(ωC))²] sets current amplitude I₀=V₀/|Z|. The difference ωL−1/(ωC) is called reactance: the signed, timing-related part of the impedance, measured in ohms. Positive and negative values describe different phase relations, not negative heating.

For a fixed voltage amplitude and positive R, current amplitude is largest when ωL=1/(ωC), so ω=1/√(LC). At this series-current resonance the reactive parts cancel. Peaks in capacitor voltage or charge need not occur at exactly the same frequency.
lessons.terms: Z, R: Impedance and resistance (Ω). Z is complex; R is positive and real. i, ω: Imaginary unit and driving angular frequency (no unit, rad/s). i²=−1. Use e^(iωt) consistently; ω>0. L, C: Inductance and capacitance (H, F). ωL and 1/(ωC) both have units ohms. I₀, V₀: Peak current and voltage amplitude (A, V). These are peak values, not RMS. |Z| is nonnegative magnitude. Bare-number arithmetic below uses the stated units; convert prefixes before combining different scales. equationGuide.meaning: Add resistance to the signed, timing-related part called reactance, ωL−1/(ωC), using the complex impedance Z. Its magnitude measures the voltage amplitude needed per unit current amplitude. Divide voltage amplitude by that magnitude to find current amplitude.

steps: Use L=1.0 H, C=0.010 F, R=4.0 Ω and peak source voltage V₀=8.0 V.

Cancellation removes reactance, not resistance.
Correct. Peak current divides by twice the resistance.

apply.text: Why must the finite steady-state amplitude formula be handled carefully at exact resonance if R=0?
apply.answer: Then the impedance magnitude is zero in this ideal algebraic expression. A lossless system driven resonantly generally accumulates oscillation energy rather than approaching a finite dissipative steady state. Initial conditions and time-dependent behavior must be treated directly.

practice.reasoning: Do not mix peak and RMS conventions. The current-amplitude peak is the specified response; other response peaks can differ. Tolerances permit decimal rounding only.

lessons.title: A changing electric field belongs in the magnetic balance
lessons.idea: A capacitor gap can contribute to Ampere’s law even when no conduction charge crosses the gap.
body: Think of a capacitor charging through wires. Conduction current carries charge in the wires, but in the ideal insulating gap no such charge crosses from one plate to the other. The electric field between the plates changes instead.

Ampere’s steady-current formula needs an extra term for a changing electric field. For a fixed surface, displacement current is I_d=ε₀ dΦ_E/dt. It is a name for this field-change term with current units, not a claim that electrons cross the vacuum gap.

The magnetic circulation around the loop depends on conduction current plus this field-change contribution, with the same loop/surface orientation. This gives consistent answers for surfaces crossing the wire or passing through the charging gap.
lessons.terms: ∮B·dℓ: Magnetic circulation (T·m). Add the along-loop magnetic field times small directed path length; the loop is closed. I_conduction, I_d: Conduction and displacement-current terms (A). The second is a field-change contribution, not charge physically crossing an ideal vacuum gap. Φ_E, t: Electric flux and time (N·m²/C, s). Use a fixed surface with normal matching the loop by the right-hand rule. μ₀, ε₀: Vacuum permeability and permittivity (H/m, F/m). Positive constants; use approximate stated numerical values when calculating. Bare-number arithmetic below uses the stated units; convert prefixes before combining different scales. lessons.title: Read four field laws as one connected map
lessons.idea: Maxwell’s equations connect charge, current and changing electric and magnetic fields.
body: The two divergence laws describe sources. Divergence is the local outward-flux balance per small volume, taught in the toolkit. Electric divergence equals charge density divided by ε₀. Magnetic divergence is zero: the classical model has no isolated magnetic-charge source.

The two curl laws describe local circulation. Curl measures a field’s local tendency to circulate. A changing magnetic field contributes to electric curl with a minus sign. Electric current and changing electric field contribute to magnetic curl.

The symbols ∂/∂t mean change with time at a fixed place. The spatial symbol ∇ combines derivatives with respect to position. These equations are not four new types of force; they state constraints that the fields and sources must satisfy together.
Boundary and starting information are still needed to solve a particular problem. A short calculation using one law is a local consistency check, not automatically a full solution of all four.
lessons.terms: E, B: Electric and magnetic field vectors (V/m (also N/C), T). The same physical fields appear throughout all four equations. ρ, J: Charge density and current-density vector (C/m³, A/m²). Rho is charge per volume; J here is current density, not the joule unit after a number. ∇·, ∇×: Divergence and curl (add inverse metres to field units). Spatial derivative operators, not multiplication by a vector called nabla. ∂/∂t: Time derivative at fixed position (adds inverse seconds). Track local time change without moving the observation point. ε₀, μ₀: Vacuum permittivity and permeability (F/m, H/m). Use the vacuum form consistently rather than mixing it with material-specific fields. Bare-number arithmetic below uses the stated units; convert prefixes before combining different scales. Unit labels: m metre, s second, C coulomb (charge), A ampere (current), V volt (energy per charge), Ω ohm (resistance), H henry (inductance), F farad (capacitance), T tesla (magnetic field), Wb weber (magnetic flux), J joule (energy), W watt (energy per second), Hz hertz (cycles per second), rad radian (angle). A symbol used as a quantity name is defined separately above.

steps: If ρ=1.77×10⁻¹¹ C/m³ and ε₀≈8.85×10⁻¹² C²/(N·m²), electric divergence is 2 N/(C·m). A spatially uniform magnetic field has zero divergence because its position derivatives are zero.

check.prompt: Does ∇·B=0 say magnetic field must be zero everywhere?
options: No, it says the local net magnetic-source balance is zero
Only a uniform field may be nonzero
explanations: Zero divergence is not the same as a zero vector field.
Correct. Nonzero magnetic fields can have zero divergence; the equation constrains their source/flux structure.
Many nonuniform magnetic fields also have zero divergence.

apply.title: Check electrostatic language
apply.text: When is saying E=−∇V alone insufficient for the full electric field?
apply.answer: In a general time-varying magnetic situation, electric curl need not be zero. A gradient-only electrostatic potential description has zero curl under ordinary smooth conditions, so it cannot alone represent that induced circulation. More general potentials or direct field equations are needed.

lessons.limits: Classical vacuum Maxwell equations with ordinary electric charges/currents and no magnetic monopoles in the model. Fields must meet appropriate regularity, boundary and initial conditions; source singularities need care.

lessons.title: A vacuum wave links electric and magnetic changes
lessons.idea: A simple electromagnetic plane wave has linked perpendicular electric and magnetic fields.
body: In an empty vacuum region, the time-dependent Maxwell equations allow wave solutions. For a wave travelling along positive x, one example has electric field along y and magnetic field along z. The fields are perpendicular to each other and to travel direction.

Write this example as E_y=E₀ cos(kx −ωt) and B_z=(E₀/c) cos(kx −ωt). E_y is the signed electric-field component along y, in V/m; B_z is the signed magnetic-field component along z, in T. E₀ is the nonnegative peak electric-field size and c is wave speed. Both cosines have the same phase: their peaks and zeros occur at the same place and time. The shared phase kx −ωt names the part of the repeating pattern: k is angular wave number in rad/m, ω is angular frequency in rad/s, x is position in metres and t is time in seconds. Each product is an angle in radians, so the subtraction is between like quantities.

The wave equation is ∂²E_y/∂x²=μ₀ε₀∂²E_y/∂t²: spatial curvature equals the constant times time curvature. Substituting a cosine pattern gives speed c=ω/k=1/√(μ₀ε₀). Maxwell’s equations also require B₀=E₀/c for this vacuum plane wave.

Wavelength λ is the distance for one cycle; frequency f is cycles each second. The same speed is c=λf. Vacuum light speed is exactly 299,792,458 m/s by SI definition; use the stated approximation 3.0×10⁸ m/s in these simple examples.
lessons.terms: c: Vacuum wave speed (m/s). This is not charge drift speed in a wire. μ₀, ε₀: Vacuum permeability and permittivity (H/m, F/m). Their product has units s²/m²; its square root is inverse speed. λ, f: Wavelength and frequency (m, hertz (Hz = cycles/s)). Lambda here means wavelength, not the earlier line-charge density. E₀, B₀: Peak electric and magnetic amplitudes (V/m, T). Amplitudes are nonnegative sizes; field directions and phase are specified separately. E_y, B_z: Signed electric and magnetic components (V/m, T). Both vary with cos(kx −ωt); y and z name perpendicular directions, not powers. k, ω, x, t: Angular wave number, angular frequency, position and time (rad/m, rad/s, m, s). The common phase kx −ωt is an angle in radians; k and ω are positive for this +x travelling wave. Bare-number arithmetic below uses the stated units; convert prefixes before combining different scales. check.prompt: In the same vacuum, a wave’s frequency doubles. What happens to wavelength?
explanations: With c fixed, λf must stay fixed.
Frequency and wavelength cannot both remain independent while speed is fixed.
Correct. λ=c/f, so doubling frequency halves wavelength.

apply.title: Check material limits
apply.text: Should B₀=E₀/c with vacuum c automatically be used unchanged inside every material?
apply.answer: No. Material response changes the wave relation and can introduce dispersion, absorption or anisotropy. Use the appropriate material model rather than importing every vacuum plane-wave relation unchanged.

lessons.title: Fields can store and carry energy
lessons.idea: Electromagnetic energy accounting includes field storage and energy flow, not only charge motion.
body: In vacuum, electric and magnetic fields have energy densities: energy per volume. Their sum is u=½ε₀E²+B²/(2μ₀), in joules per cubic metre. Here E and B mean field magnitudes, so their squares are nonnegative.

The Poynting vector S=(E×B)/μ₀ describes electromagnetic energy flow per area, in watts per square metre. Its direction follows the cross product. It is not the number of charged particles crossing that area.

For a sinusoidal vacuum plane wave, electric and magnetic energies are equal at each phase. Average intensity is ⟨S⟩=½ε₀cE₀² when E₀ is the peak electric amplitude. Angle brackets mean average over a cycle; the half comes from averaging the squared sinusoid.

Accelerating charges and changing currents can generate radiation by exchanging energy with the fields. The simple plane-wave intensity formula does not describe every field near those sources; near-field energy can also move back and forth rather than radiate away.
lessons.equation: u = ½ε₀E² + B²/(2μ₀);  S = (E×B)/μ₀;  ⟨S⟩ = ½ε₀cE₀² for a sinusoidal vacuum plane wave

Use magnitudes in u; use vectors in the cross product for S. S, ⟨S⟩: Instantaneous energy-flow vector and average intensity (W/m²). For this plane wave the average points along travel. W is watts, not work quantity W. ε₀, μ₀, c, E₀: Vacuum constants, speed and peak electric amplitude (F/m, H/m, m/s, V/m). The average formula assumes a sinusoid and a peak—not RMS—amplitude. Bare-number arithmetic below uses the stated units; convert prefixes before combining different scales. steps: Use E₀=20 V/m, ε₀≈8.85×10⁻¹² F/m and c≈3.0×10⁸ m/s for a sinusoidal vacuum plane wave.
Average intensity is½ε₀cE₀²≈0.531 W/m². At a field maximum, total energy density is u=ε₀E₀²≈3.54×10⁻⁹ J/m³ because the electric and magnetic parts are equal.

check.prompt: Peak E₀ doubles in the same vacuum plane-wave model. How does average intensity change?
options: It becomes four times as large
explanations: Correct. Intensity is proportional to E₀², so doubling amplitude multiplies it by four.
That would miss the square in the amplitude relation.
Increasing amplitude increases intensity in this model.

apply.title: Distinguish average from peak
apply.text: Why would inserting an RMS electric amplitude into½ε₀cE₀² without adjusting the formula give a wrong intensity?
apply.answer: The displayed formula expects peak amplitude. A sinusoid’s RMS amplitude is peak divided by√2, so average intensity is ε₀cE_RMS² without the extra half. Mixing conventions would count the averaging factor twice.

lessons.title: Choose the model before choosing the equation
lessons.idea: A useful equation matches the source, geometry, time dependence and quantity being asked for.
body: Start with the question: force on a charge, field at a point, potential difference, circuit current or energy transfer? These are connected quantities, but none is a substitute for all the others.

Next state the conditions. Point-charge formulas need an appropriate source model. A Gaussian surface gives a simple field value only with enough symmetry. A resistor-only current rule may fail during an inductive transient.

Finally check time dependence. Electrostatic E=−∇V and zero closed-loop electric work do not describe general induction. A changing field/circuit needs the relevant time-dependent relation and initial conditions.
After calculating, test a limit and the units. A result can have correct units while using the wrong assumptions, as when a final changing rate is substituted for a whole-interval average.
lessons.equation: F = qE;  ΔV = −∫ E·dℓ in electrostatics;  V_R = IR for an ohmic resistor

ΔV, dℓ: Potential difference and directed path step (V, m). The electrostatic integral has a specified start/end and gradient-field assumptions. V_R, I, R: Resistor voltage drop, current and resistance (V, A, Ω). Use a consistent passive sign convention; this is not the voltage-current rule for every device. lessons.title: Connect a field estimate to a discharge
lessons.idea: One setup can require different models for its geometry, energy and time response.
body: Use an ideal parallel-plate capacitor near its central region, where field is approximately uniform and fringing is neglected. Voltage V across gap d gives field magnitude E=V/d. Capacitance C gives stored charge Q=CV and energy U=½CV².

After disconnecting the ideal charging source, close an ideal discharge path through resistance R. Voltage then decays as V(t)=V₀e^(−t/(RC)). The time constant RC describes voltage/charge decay, while stored energy depends on voltage squared.

A very small probe does not significantly disturb the capacitor field in this model. Its electric force is qE, with signed probe charge q. Do not confuse that probe q with the much larger plate charge Q.

Treat charging, the chosen field observation and discharging as separate stated intervals. Energy stored before discharge transfers to the resistor in the ideal closed circuit; the fixed-capacitance field approximation is part of the setup.
lessons.terms: C, R, d: Capacitance, resistance and plate gap (F, Ω, m). C names capacitance here, while C after a charge value is coulombs. Components are ideal and fixed. Q, q: Plate-charge magnitude and signed probe charge (coulombs (C)). The small probe is assumed not to disturb the source field. V₀, V(t), E, F: Initial/current voltage, field and probe force (V, V, V/m, N). Choose a positive field direction before giving a force sign. t, U: Elapsed discharge time and stored energy (s, J). RC is in seconds. The voltage amplitude—not energy—has time constant RC. Bare-number arithmetic below uses the stated units; convert prefixes before combining different scales. example.title: An original field-and-discharge case
steps: Use C=4 nF, R=2.5 MΩ, initial voltage V₀=5 V and gap d=2 mm. Here n=10⁻⁹, M=10⁶ and mm=10⁻³ m.
Plate charge is 20 nC, initial energy is 50 nJ, time constant is 0.010 s, and central field magnitude is 2,500 V/m. A+2 pC probe, with p=10⁻¹², feels 5×10⁻⁹ N along the field.
At t=RC ln 2≈0.00693 s, voltage halves to 2.5 V. The natural logarithm ln 2≈0.693 reverses the exponential. Stored energy is then one quarter,12.5 nJ;37.5 nJ has transferred to the ideal resistor.

check.prompt: When the voltage has fallen to half its starting value, what fraction of the initial capacitor energy remains?
explanations: Energy is proportional to voltage squared at fixed capacitance.
A passive discharge decreases stored capacitor energy.
Correct. (1/2)²=1/4, so half the voltage leaves a quarter of the energy.

apply.title: Explain a limiting case
apply.text: In this ideal model, what should happen at very long discharge time?
apply.answer: Voltage, plate-charge magnitude, central field and probe force approach zero. Capacitor energy also approaches zero, with the initial stored energy transferred to the resistor. These limits assume a closed discharge path and ignore leakage through other routes, dielectric changes and residual effects.

lessons.title: Use flux, current and energy in the right order
lessons.idea: A changed field can induce a current, but its heating must still have an energy source.
body: For a fixed single loop in a spatially uniform magnetic field normal to its plane, flux is Φ_B=BA. Here A is loop area. If the orientation and area stay fixed, the flux change comes from the field change.

Find induced emf from the signed flux rate first. If resistance dominates and self-inductance is negligible, use I=ℰ/R. The sign describes current direction; heating power I²R is nonnegative regardless of that sign.

For a constant rate of flux change, this approximation gives constant emf and current during that interval. Heat transferred to the resistor is power times interval duration. The external source changing the magnetic field supplies the required energy transfer.

Before marking this lesson complete, explain why the fixed-loop flux rule, resistor approximation and steady-rate assumption apply. Correct arithmetic without these conditions is not evidence of independent model selection.
lessons.terms: A, ΔB, Δt: Fixed area, signed field change and interval duration (m², T, s). The field is uniform and normal; its rate is constant during this interval. ℰ, I, R: Induced emf, signed current and resistance (V, A, Ω). Positive loop direction matches the chosen positive normal by the right-hand rule. P, Q_heat: Resistor heating power and transferred heat (W, J). Q_heat is energy here, not the charge Q used in other lessons. Its subscript distinguishes the quantity. Bare-number arithmetic below uses the stated units; convert prefixes before combining different scales. example.title: A fresh single-loop case
steps: Let A=0.020 m² and R=4.0 Ω. Signed normal B rises uniformly from 0.10 T to 0.40 T in 0.30 s.
Emf is −0.020 V and current is −0.0050 A. The minus signs mean opposite the chosen positive loop direction.
Heating power is(0.0050 A)²(4.0 Ω)=1.0×10⁻⁴ W. Over 0.30 s, heat is 3.0×10⁻⁵ J; the external changing-field source participates in that energy transfer.

check.prompt: With the same constant emf, resistance doubles. How does resistor heating power change in this approximation?
explanations: Correct. Current halves, so I²R becomes one quarter times two: half the original power. Equivalently P=ℰ²/R.
Holding emf fixed is not the same as holding current fixed.
Both current and power depend on the resistance under a fixed emf.

apply.title: Name a failure condition
apply.text: What could make the simple current formula I=ℰ/R inadequate here?
apply.answer: Significant self-inductance makes current respond over time instead of instantly following emf. Changing loop shape, nonuniform fields or nonlinear resistance also require revising the stated model. Explain the replacement equation and initial conditions before calculating.
